note:
In the prose prologue, the narrator provides the reader with essential background information for understanding the central poetic speeches. There are two basic points being made: what befalls Job is not a consequence of sinful behavior on his part, and all that occurs is under the sovereign control of God.

**1:1–5** The prologue (chs. 1; 2) begins with a depiction of Job as blessed by and devoted to his God.

**1:1 Uz.** An extended region east of Judah, perhaps on the edge of the desert but conducive to raising crops (v. 14) and livestock (v. 3). Job is not a nomad but an elder in a major town (29:7).

**Job.** The meaning of his name is uncertain, but see note on 6:27; 13:24. There is no mention of his family line, implying he is not an Israelite. His standing before God is based not on inherited privilege but on personal commitment.

**blameless and upright.** “Blameless” means acting with integrity, springing from a wholehearted commitment to God. “Upright” describes one whose conduct is habitually ethically correct. This is ordinary language and means not that Job was sinless but that he is genuine in his religious profession.

**feared God and turned away from evil.** Job’s character embodies awe and respect for God, shunning all who would offend Him. This verdict is endorsed by God in 1:8 and 2:3.

Job is blessed with a large family. Retribution theology (Introduction: Genre) would argue that this is a sign of Job’s righteousness and that its loss a sign of his sin. As this book will reveal, however, this kind of retribution theology is far too simplistic to explain God’s providential dealings with his people.
Patriarchal wealth is measured by numbers of livestock (see Gen. 30:43).
There was a prearranged program for these festivities, perhaps in connection with their birthdays.

Job is rightly concerned for the spiritual welfare of his children.

**offer burnt offerings.** By this means of grace the patriarch Job, like Abraham (Gen. 15:9, 10), fills the role of priest for the family, consecrating his children to God. In the epilogue Job again plays an intercessory role (42:8, 9).

**cursed God in their hearts.** The Hebrew reads lit. “blessed God,” but that is a euphemism to avoid uttering “curse” next to “God.” Cursing God is a sin in which Job himself will be tested (v. 11).

The writer reveals the developments in heaven and their consequences on earth that lead to Job’s suffering, first regarding his possessions and family (vv. 6–22) and then his physical well-being (2:1–10).

**1:6–12** The first of two scenes in heaven depicting the divine council and focusing on an encounter between the Lord (Yahweh) and Satan. As the text note indicates, throughout chs. 1; 2 Satan is not a proper name but a descriptive term meaning “the adversary.” While some argue that he is merely an angel who functions as the Lord’s observer of affairs on earth, “also” (1:6) indicates that his presence is intrusive. Additional information will be revealed in later ages about his character, but here Satan is obviously more than a prosecutor. He opposes the will of God, in keeping with the role of the serpent in Gen. 3. In v. 9 he questions Job’s religious motivation. The use of Yahweh, the covenant name of God, throughout chs. 1; 2 (also in 38:1; 40:1; 42) indicates that God is in a loving and merciful covenant relationship with Job.

**1:6 Satan.** See theological note “Satan.” He is not a free agent but needs divine permission to proceed.
It is the Lord who initiates the interchange. Satan constantly scrutinizes human affairs to identify the vulnerable.
Job is honored by God, who approves of him as a true and faithful servant, i.e., one keeping the solemn oaths of the covenant relationship. It is God, not Satan, who singles out Job for testing.
Satan does not dispute Job’s integrity but argues that Job’s conduct is motivated by what he gets out of it rather than by a sincere attachment to the Lord.
Satan also insinuates that the only way God can get people to worship Him is by bribing them with protection and prosperity.
The question is whether Job, who was so sensitive to the possibility of his children’s cursing God, will now sin that way himself.
The adversary is allowed to test Job, but at this point, only with regard to his possessions and family. Satan’s activities are restricted to what is permitted by the Lord.

Satan delivers an assault on Job’s possessions, servants, and, climactically, his children. Each time he leaves a single survivor to bring word to Job, but while one messenger is still relating his catastrophic news, another comes to tell of a further dire blow. Even so, Job remains steadfast in his belief that God is good.
The Sabeans were a tribe from the south Arabian desert. The Chaldeans were at this time a marauding tribe from north Arabia. Their descendants later became the rulers of Babylon., 17

Job utters a wisdom poem that portrays the discernment of quiet submission to the secret will of God. Everything belongs to the creator who gave it. God’s people must praise Him for whatever He does with what is His. The word “blessed” (v. 21) is the same used in v. 11 for “cursed.” By employing it here, the author is emphasizing how Job, though grief-stricken, has frustrated Satan’s predictions in v. 11. However, v. 22 implies the testing is not yet over.
Further developments in heaven—another round of accusations from Satan—precede more suffering for Job on earth.

verse_quote: holds fast his integrity ... without reason.
note: “Integrity” lit. “blamelessness.” The sudden change from the words of 1:6–8 at the end of 2:1–3 shows how the adversary, who has lost the first round, is humiliated by God through a bit of irony. The same word (“for no reason,” 1:9) Satan had used to accuse Job is used here, translated “without reason.” It is the adversary who has done wrong, not Job.

Satan suggests that even Job’s statement of faith in 1:21 is nothing but a ploy. Job is willing to sacrifice anything for his own skin. If God will only stretch out His hand and strike Job’s body, then he will curse God to His face.

God permits the adversary to be used as His instrument to strike Job, a fact that bears on the problem of evil. Satan, as a creature, is reined in. He is allowed to go only as far as God permits. The word translated “spare” can be translated “safeguard”; it would appear that Satan is being held responsible for Job’s life.

Notwithstanding Satan’s divinely permitted (and divinely limited) attacks on Job’s body, Job holds firm to his conviction that God is praiseworthy.

**2:7 loathsome sores.** We have no way of knowing the exact nature of the disease that affects Job’s skin. But it is disfiguring and painful.
Perhaps by trial and error the ancients learned that the ashes were a place where disease would not spread. Or it may simply have been a way of lamenting.

Job’s wife is unaware of God’s guarantee that Job’s life would not be taken. She does not doubt his integrity and may be speaking out of a misplaced sympathy, considering death to be preferable to the agony her husband is suffering. Whatever her motives, her intervention increases the pressure on Job to succumb to the temptation.

The Hebrew word for “foolish” or “fool” has to do with faithlessness and religious apostasy, as in Ps. 14:1 (see also Ps. 53:1). It is more an ethical judgment than an intellectual one.

**Job did not sin with his lips.** This stress on the purity of Job’s speech is an anticipation of the contrast that will come in the dialogue, where Job’s words are less pure.

In the final paragraph of the prologue, Job’s friends arrive to comfort him in the midst of his terrible suffering. They live in different localities, and the time taken for news to reach them, to make arrangements for the visit, and to travel to Job implies that his sufferings were already prolonged when they arrived (see 7:3). They are introduced as a group, and they share a similar outlook. Although they will become highly critical of Job, their visit is well-intentioned.

An indication of the severity of Job’s physical affliction.

**wept ... robes ... sprinkled dust.** Cultural expressions of distress and anxiety.

verse_quote: they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him.
note: This behavior, tied to the number of completeness (seven), expresses the most intense form of grief they can display. For the practice of mourning seven days over the dead, see Gen. 50:10. By conforming to Near Eastern protocol, which demands that Job should be the first to break the silence, the friends exhibit sympathy and wisdom in a way that they fail to do when they actually do speak.

Job breaks the weeklong silence with a fiercely emotional lamentation. He expresses the same kind of depression that overtook the psalmist (Ps. 88) and Jeremiah (Jer. 20:14, 15), whose bitter lament is similar to Job’s in language.

Job does not curse God, but he goes so far as to question God’s wisdom in giving him life. It is also significant that although Job is mentally and spiritually at the breaking point, it does not cross his mind to take his own life.

Job wishes for the nonexistence of the day of his birth. This curse would reverse creation and introduce darkness rather than light into that day. If the day had never existed, then neither would Job.
Refers to the night of v. 3; the thought is that it would be better for Job if he had never been conceived.

Job refers to enchanters who claim they can rouse the seven-headed monster of the deep (41:1 note). The thought may be that the monster will cause an eclipse by swallowing the sun or the moon. No sun would indicate no calendar day on which Job’s birth could occur.
That is, of the night of his conception. The morning stars are to be extinguished rather than usher in the dawn. “Eyelids of the morning” personifies dawn, a dawn that Job wishes had never come.

Verses 3–10 are set in the form of curses, while these are rhetorical questions, perhaps uttered more musingly. Job gives vent to his frustration, asking why he did not die at or just after birth (vv. 11, 12, 16) so as to escape his present agony. Since that did not happen, in vexation he moves on to ask rhetorically why he should not now experience premature death (vv. 20, 23).
Either those of his mother as she holds him in her lap or of his father who acknowledges him as his legitimate son (see Gen. 50:23).

At this early stage of divine revelation, Job’s view of existence after death is colored by what will be absent in death. There will no longer be the striving of the mighty after greater achievements (vv. 14, 15) or harassment from the wicked (v. 17) or maltreatment of the oppressed (v. 18). Death, the great leveler (v. 19), brings an end to earthly agony—including that of Job., 17
Job is speaking under intense emotional pressure; his thought here is not consecutive but reverts to the theme of vv. 11, 12.

Job generalizes from his situation to include all who suffer. Unlike 1:10, the divine hedge in v. 23 is one that prevents an afflicted individual from seeing a way of escape from his situation. Job questions how living is worthwhile for one engulfed by misery.

**3:20 the bitter in soul.** Those experiencing intense inward vexation and distress about God’s providential dealings with them (7:11; 10:1; 27:2 and notes).
That is, an experience of physical suffering and spiritual desolation such as has overwhelmed Job.

The weeklong silence has been broken by Job’s anguished outburst (ch. 3), after which his friends can no longer keep silent. They speak in turn, probably in order of seniority, and Job responds to each contribution. All the speakers accept a simplistic “retribution principle,” whereby God controls the world by punishing anyone who sins and rewards whoever does what is right. Job’s friends, however, hold that the reverse is also true: whoever suffers has sinned and whoever is blessed is righteous. As such, there is a one-to-one correspondence between sin and suffering; since Job is suffering so greatly, he has sinned greatly. At first they just hint at this (5:8; 8:6; 11:14), but when Job fails to accept their analysis, they become more open and ferocious in their attacks. Though ultimately it is true that God punishes (impenitent) sinners and rewards (those whom He mercifully declares to be) righteous people, Job’s friends err in believing that every instance of suffering is an application of this principle.

**4:1–5:27** The name _Eliphaz_ means “my God is gold,” but that does not contribute to understanding the present account. He comes from Teman in Edom, a locale with a reputation for wisdom (Jer. 49:7).

Eliphaz is the least caustic of Job’s three friends, at least in his first speech. Compare these opening words, which assume Job is innocent (v. 7), with 22:1–11, where he is fully convinced Job is getting what he deserves. Job is complimented for being a wisdom teacher who in the past has helped the discouraged (vv. 3, 4), but in v. 5 he is warned lest he fails in his suffering to apply to himself what he once taught others.

Lit. “your fear.” Eliphaz acknowledges the genuine piety that controls Job’s life (see 1:1). His question is put in such a way as to encourage Job that his present distress will not last. According to Eliphaz’s theology, any interruption of the good fortune of the pious can only be temporary.

Eliphaz assures Job that God will preserve the righteous and bring the wicked to an early grave. However, even from the death of Abel (Gen. 4:8–11; 1 John 3:12), and especially in the death of Christ, it is evident that the retribution principle is not the only factor determining God’s providential rule.

Eliphaz bases his advice on personal observation (5:3 note; 15:17 note), but personal observation and experience is a limited basis for wisdom.

**sow trouble reap the same.** Such wisdom cannot be denied, but does it apply to Job? Is retribution imposed as immediately as Eliphaz implies? This approach also fails to allow for the activity of divine grace, where we reap what we have not sown.
Five different words are used to describe lions. Their strong appearance does not mean that they can thwart the operation of universal law. No more can the wicked escape divine judgment., 11

Although Eliphaz is unsure of the identity of the one who visited him in his night vision (v. 16), he is certain he received authoritative, supernatural revelation. It is always necessary, however, to test the genuineness of such an experience (see 1 John 4:1).

It is unclear where the message Eliphaz heard ends. The ESV extends the quotation to the end of v. 21, but it may only consist of v. 17, in which case the remaining verses expand on what Eliphaz heard.

**4:17 in the right before God.** Although this may also be translated “more righteous than God” (text note), that rendering is implausible in this context. Eliphaz is not (yet) implying that Job has become so conceited. The rhetorical questions emphasize human moral inadequacy. Whether weak (“mortal man”) or strong (“man” at the height of his powers), “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23). Job therefore has no ground for complaint against God (see 9:1 for Job’s rejoinder).
Even angels are not exempt from divine criticism and rebuke, so Job should not expect to avoid it.
A reference to the human body (10:9; 33:6; cf. Gen. 2:7). Job shares the frailty of all mankind, and his departure will attract as little attention as a moth being swatted.
That is, their death is without any purpose and therefore meaningless. They “perish forever” (v. 20) with no rationale for their lives.

Eliphaz asserts that no other being, human or angelic, is in a position to extend help to Job as he endures the troubles that are common to mankind. The idea of mediatorial assistance is a theme that Job will repeatedly take up later (9:33; 16:19, 20; 19:25).

**5:1 To which of the holy ones will you turn.** None of the “sons of God” (1:6), the holy angels, would dare to help Job or could do so in the light of the assessment of 4:18.

An intense emotional reaction to circumstances, such as that displayed by Job in ch. 3. “Jealousy,” envy of the lot of others, perhaps reflects Job’s desire to have been stillborn (3:16). Although Eliphaz is speaking in general terms, there is no doubt that he is alleging Job’s behavior to be that of “the fool” and “the simple,” wisdom language for those lacking spiritual insight.
Eliphaz views himself as approving of, and participating in, the retribution that will inevitably overturn the fortunes of the wicked.
Even though it is presented as a proverbial truth, the implied reference to Job’s family is still insensitive (see 1:18, 19).
Eliphaz’s point is that trouble does not spring up spontaneously like a weed but is inevitably reaped by those who sow it.

Lit. “the sons of Resheph fly upward.” Resheph was the god of pestilence, lightning, and destruction. A similar idiom is used in Song 8:6, where love is described as “flashes of fire.” In other places the idiom is used for bolts of lightning (Ps. 78:48) and of pestilence (Deut. 32:24; Hab. 3:5). From the day an individual is born, any activity generates frustration and woe as inevitably as a fire generates sparks.

Since Eliphaz cannot conceive of another being intervening effectively, he advises Job to appeal to God for assistance. In general, this is good advice, but implicit here is the misplaced assumption that Job has deliberately sinned in a heinous manner. For Job to seek God would require repentance and a request for forgiveness, but Job knows that he has not acted in a reprehensible fashion.

**5:8 commit my cause.** Hints at a legal interpretation of the dialogues (9:3 note).

Paul cites the first line of this verse in 1 Cor. 3:19 to establish divine superiority over those who consider themselves to be wise. The problem with Job’s counselors is not so much ignorance of the truth as the wrongheaded and partial application of it.
A reference to slander (see v. 21).

Eliphaz informs Job why he should not despise God’s dealings with him. Whoever accepts divine correction will be restored and blessed (see Prov. 3:11, 12). This reference to the disciplinary nature of human suffering is the only place in the speeches of the three counselors where the subject is even broached. Job is only at the first stage of a process that will lead to healing and recovery (v. 18). In vv. 19–22, the second line reinforces the theme of the first line.

**5:17 the Almighty.** The first of thirty-one times that “the Almighty” is used in Job to render the Hebrew term _Shaddai_ (Gen. 17:1 note). The title is most commonly thought to be derived from an Akkadian word meaning “mountain” and conveys the thought that God is mountain-like, that is, enduring, imposing, majestic, and awe inspiring. The rendering “Almighty” dates back to the Septuagint and associates this name of God with his supreme power and total sovereignty over creation.
A poetic expression meaning “many.”

verse_quote: in league with the stones of the field.
note: This may well be figurative language describing an Edenic condition before the curse imposed after the fall. Job’s physical environment would no longer frustrate his attempts at cultivation. Alternatively, some read this as “in league with the offspring of the field” to reflect the other side of the parallelism that reads, “the beasts of the field shall be at peace with you.” Since wild animals often kill domestic animals, this fits the context, where in v. 22 Eliphaz says Job has no need to fear the beasts of the earth.
Considering that Job has lost all his children, the statement is both unnecessary and cruel.
At this point neither Job nor Eliphaz can imagine that this statement will come true for Job (see 42:16, 17).

verse_quote: this we have searched out; it is true.
note: Eliphaz commends to Job the conclusions reached by wisdom teachers (including Eliphaz) regarding the blessings that come to the repentant. However, the generalization, which is an expression of simplistic retribution theology, is not invariably true, and, crucially, his advice to Job to repent is based on a complete misunderstanding of the origin of Job’s sufferings.

Job often does not directly respond to the arguments of his friends. Here he begins with introspective soliloquy before upbraiding Eliphaz for uttering presumptuous, insensitive, not to mention false, words about him (6:14–30); then in ch. 7 he addresses his complaint to God.
Job speaks out of his anguish and argues that if the extent of his suffering were accurately assessed, it would be seen as more than sufficient to warrant his complaints.

verse_quote: my words have been rash. For the arrows of the Almighty are in me.
note: Job excuses his raging by fantasizing that God has become his enemy. He shares Eliphaz’s presupposition that this suffering is divinely imposed, but Job does not know why. 4
Job’s questions expect a negative answer. The vehemence of his speech has arisen from his distressing circumstances.
Eliphaz has offered him no real food (v. 5), i.e., words of comfort. What was supposed to be good food (words of comfort from friends) has made Job sick., 7

verse_quote: Oh that I might have my request.
note: Job does not contemplate suicide. Rather, he affirms that the only comfort left to him is the exquisite release from pain that death, sent by God, would bring. He strongly affirms continued faith in God. This passage shows that Job believes in a blissful afterlife.
As a weaver cuts a thread, so would God bring Job’s earthly existence to an end.

verse_quote: I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
note: The first of Job’s affirmations of innocence (see 9:21; 16:17; 27:6). He has lived by God’s words (commands) and is unaware of how he has offended God and brought such suffering on himself. Such a declaration does not ring true as far as his friends are concerned. For them Job’s suffering clearly proves otherwise.
In a series of rhetorical questions, Job affirms that he is drained of strength and unable to endure much longer.

Job complains that his friends have acted improperly in not displaying toward him kindness or steadfast love, that is, the protection and assistance appropriate to a committed relationship. Even though Job knows he is innocent, he still needs companionship and sympathy. Their response has been deficient.

Intensifies their insensitivity. It reminds one of Judas (John 13:18) or the disciples (Matt. 26:40).

**torrent-bed.** In the rainy season a wadi turns into a raging torrent, but in summer, when water is needed, it dries up. In his extended metaphor (6:15–20), Job pictures desert travelers seeking water from such wadis, only to be disappointed.

Plural, referring to the three counselors. Even though Job had not sought costly favors from them, they were afraid to help him. They would rather maintain their theology than allow for an exception. Such an admission would deprive them of the satisfaction they derive from their ability to analyze the circumstances of life.
Job asks his friends to give him real help by providing direct evidence of the wrongdoing they allege he must have committed.

The difference between Job and his friends is summed up here. The speeches of the friends are formally correct but do not necessarily apply to Job. Indeed, the friends falsely accuse Job of having lived a sinful life. Job insists on speaking honest words about his life: he has never forsaken God or lived in a profligate way.
Later, Job will speak of his loving care for the fatherless (31:16–22). His name possibly means “without a father.”
Lit. “is in it.” The “it” is their insistence that he is suffering for his sins. Either he or they must be wrong.
In vv. 6, 7 Job spoke of their words as bad food. Here he pleads that they change what they are feeding him.

Job reverts to soliloquy in which he at first reflects on the harsh lot of mankind in general (vv. 1, 2) before describing his own circumstances (vv. 3–6). Whereas the shadows of evening bring relief to the slave toiling under the sun and a hired hand can expect due payment, in his despair Job has nothing to look forward to (v. 6).

**7:1 hard service.** The terminology often refers to military service, but here it describes the inescapable rigors of life in general.
Job’s malady may be a combination of diseases. Repulsive symptoms, however, have appeared all over his skin, the largest and most sensitive bodily organ.
The term “hope” skillfully extends the weaving metaphor of the preceding line; there is a similarly spelled word meaning “cord” or “thread” (see Josh. 2:18).

The singular form of the verb “remember” (v. 7) shows that God is now being addressed as Job sets out the brevity of earthly existence for himself and for mankind generally. Comparable sentiments about life as “a breath” are found in the Psalms (see Pss. 39:4–6; 62:9; 144:3, 4). But reflecting on human transience turns the psalmists to God, whereas Job reacts bleakly and holds out no hope for himself.

**7:7 never again see good.** Worse than pain is the loss of hope for a return to health.
The language of appearance. Job is not developing a doctrine but merely stating what all observe. Later, Job will show he believes in the possibility of resurrection (14:12–15).

Job refuses to go quietly and sets out the grounds of his complaint regarding God’s unremitting and harsh treatment.

**7:11 will not restrain my mouth.** Like the psalmist who had to give vent to his emotionally distraught feelings (Ps. 39:3), Job insists on complaining out of his “bitterness of soul” (3:20 note). Note that here he complains to God, not to man.

The Hebrew uses “sea” as a proper name here without the definite article. This is poetic language for the boisterous Canaanite deity Yam (sea). Job does not worship Yam, but he knows the story about him.

**a sea monster.** Possibly a reference to Tiamat, who, according to Babylonian myth, was overcome and held captive by the god Marduk to create the ordered world of human existence. Job complains that God is treating him in a disproportionately harsh fashion.

**set a guard.** An instance of dramatic irony in the light of the prologue, esp. 2:6. God had been guarding Job but not in the restrictive manner Job thought.
Job imagines that God is actually doing all this. The reader knows from the prologue that God permitted Satan to do it. Yet that permission is within God’s sovereign ordination.
Job sees death as the way out, but Satan has not been permitted to go that far, nor would death serve Satan’s purpose of getting Job to curse God to His face.
Again, Job imagines that God is the one who torments him. We know from the prologue, however, that God has a high and holy purpose in permitting Satan to touch Job.

verse_quote: What is man, that you make so much of him.
note: A similar thought is expressed positively in Pss. 8:4 and 144:3. The psalmist marvels that God cares so much for the creature He has made in His own image. But Job, in his distress, wishes that God would leave him alone.
Subject to scrutiny and examination (23:10 note).
Job thinks God is too critical and eager to find faults. For what sin is God punishing him so severely?

Though Job will stress his integrity (i.e., his honest commitment to godliness and righteousness), he never denies being a sinner. Job argues that if he has committed such heinous sin as to warrant his suffering, God should deal with the matter immediately and forgive him. That God does not implies that He must prefer to punish rather than forgive. But Job’s agony is so intense that without immediate relief, his death seems inevitable.

This short contribution reveals Bildad to be a blunt and unfeeling person. He has failed to hear Job’s cry for compassion (6:13, 14, 26). His message to Job is forthright: he and his family have received what they deserve. Now if only Job will repent of the shameless deeds that brought on this disaster, he can be restored to even greater prosperity and happiness than he had before.

**8:1–7** Bildad reveals his impatience at Job’s attempts to clear himself and at his failure to accept the counsel offered to him.

**8:1 Bildad the Shuhite.** Bildad’s name may be an Aramaic compound of the names of two gods, Baal and Hadad. Shuah was a son of Abraham and Keturah (Gen. 25:2), whose descendants were located in northeast Arabia. Like the other counselors, Bildad is not of Israelite descent.

A strong accusation, picking up on and intensifying Job’s expression in 6:26. It is unlike the tone of Eliphaz, who attempted a soft approach at first (4:2). On the basis of Job’s suffering, Bildad is sure that Job’s protestations are all bluster, with no real content.
Bildad rebuts what he infers is Job’s position, that God is unjust. “Pervert” conveys the thought of twisting what is straight out of shape.
Bildad expresses himself with a veneer of sensitivity, though it is clear what he really thinks. Those who offend God die, and conversely those who die young must have offended God grievously.

verse_quote: if you are pure and upright.
note: In Bildad’s mind, God has mercy only when human beings deserve it. Mercy, however, cannot ever be deserved. In Bildad’s interpretation of the situation, he is offering Job a way out of his misery. He not only urges repentance but also points to good works as the basis of enjoying God’s favor.

Eliphaz appealed to revelation as his authority, even though that revelation was somewhat enigmatic (4:12–17). Bildad appeals to human tradition. He has not invented his theology but inherited it from former generations whose views were accorded great respect in the ancient Near East.

Bildad sets out in general terms traditional teaching regarding conduct and rewards. Illustrations drawn from the natural world show the invariable connection between cause and effect. Without water, plants cannot grow.

This Hebrew word occurs eight times in Job (8:13; 13:16; 15:34; 17:8; 20:5; 27:8; 34:30; 36:13) and refers to someone who is arrogant and defiant in rebellion against God and so is profane or defiled by sin. Obviously, Bildad sees Job as a case in point.
The hope of the godless provides no more substantial a foundation for life than a spider’s web., 15
The description is of a prolific plant with shallow roots. If such superficial support is removed, the plant collapses. Similarly, the success of the wicked soon passes.

verse_quote: God will not reject a blameless man.
note:
The heart of Bildad’s theology of suffering. As standard wisdom it is not wrong. Ps. 1:6 teaches that the Lord cares about the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked shall perish. Bildad’s error is that Job’s suffering indicates Job is godless.

**take the hand of evildoers.** An action associated with providing guidance and security.

Job does not give an item-by-item rejoinder to all that Bildad has said, though he does display an awareness of Bildad’s points. Job starts with a discourse on God’s power and wisdom (9:1–13) but shifts to questioning His justice (9:14–35). In 9:28–31 he begins to direct his words to God, which continues through ch. 10.

Job makes extensive use of legal terminology because he considers that God is treating him as guilty of some offense. Job is unable to mount an effective challenge against God because of the power God possesses.

**9:2 Truly I know that it is so.** Job has no quarrel with Bildad’s view that God punishes the wicked and cares for the righteous (Ps. 1:6). But why then is he suffering? Job accepts the retribution principle just as much as Bildad and the other friends, which is why he has an insoluble problem. Convinced as he is of his integrity and acutely aware of his suffering, Job’s presuppositions can lead him to conclude only that God has unfairly perceived him as guilty.

**But how can a man be in the right before God?** Job is concerned about the impossible task of trying to establish a case before, and against, God.

This term introduces a significant theme in Job—initiating litigation against God. “To contend” is to lodge a complaint or accusation against someone. Job is uncertain if this is possible to do against God. He does not anticipate that God Himself will be his cross-examiner at the end of his story (38:3; 40:7).

The creative initiative and overwhelming power of the God whom Job worships far exceed anything attributed by pagan mythology to their gods, singly or combined. Job reverently asserts that the one true God is unique and supreme. Job is challenged to learn this lesson anew in chs. 38–41. Here Job’s perception of God’s power leads him to conclude that he is incapable of mounting a successful challenge to God’s ways.
The earth is described poetically as having subterranean architecture.
The reference is to an eclipse of the sun and the disappearance of certain stars over the seasons.
The poetic figures in this verse refer to God’s creation and control of the forces of nature.
Job refers to various constellations, emphasizing God’s creative power and thus the foolishness of contending with Him (see 38:31, 32).

Job poignantly begs for the friendship and empathy he needs, but nothing of the sort is possible from his counselors, who have only added to his misery.

**the hand of God.** Refers to God’s acting powerfully, often on behalf of His people, but here perceived by Job to be acting against him., 22

Job’s mood swings for a little from the depths of his misery, and in faith he desires that his cause will be vindicated by a permanent memorial (vv. 23, 24). He confidently affirms that his situation will be rectified through the activity of a “Redeemer” (vv. 25–27). The text is variously understood, and the precise meaning of his affirmation is disputed. Many scholars deny that the passage has any eschatological significance. They argue that Job does not anticipate bodily resurrection but instead yearns for no more than to see God before he dies so that God will vindicate him. Such a conclusion is often based on the perception that belief in an afterlife did not arise until much later in the OT. This view is improbable. Even though in the earliest times not much information was disclosed about life after death, an awareness of it existed, albeit dimly (e.g., Gen. 5:24). Under the pressure of his experience, Job’s vision has moved from the world around him to future realities. Even if v. 25 is not understood as direct messianic prophecy, there can be no doubt that these words are an expression of indomitable faith that rises above the immediately perceptible because of trust in God. His words are ultimately fulfilled in Christ.

**19:23, 24** Job has an important message that he wants permanently inscribed for posterity. Through the inspiration of the Spirit, his words are preserved for all time in the Bible (see Mark 14:9).

**19:24 engraved in the rock.** The probable process in view involves chiseling out letters and then filling them with lead to produce a permanent public memorial, rather than the more private rec­ord of a “book” or, better yet, “scroll” (v. 23).

verse_quote: I know that my Redeemer lives.
note:
The Hebrew word translated “Redeemer” can also be rendered “avenger,” “guarantor,” “vindicator,” or “kinsman-redeemer” (Ruth 2:20 note). Job’s words are clear, but from his perspective, who will help him? The prologue reveals that God is not Job’s enemy. Indeed, God will become his vindicator (42:7). Job elsewhere seems to think of the Redeemer as a third party (16:19–21).

**at the last he will stand upon the earth.** In Job’s mind, this vindicator will be both heavenly (16:19) and earthly (able to stand on the earth). “Stand upon the earth” is literally “rise upon dust.” In this context, where death is prominent, Job imagines that after his death, his vindicator will bear witness to others regarding his integrity.

Job is aware that the disease racking his frame will prove fatal if left unchecked.

**in my flesh.** The meaning of the preposition “in” (lit. “from”) could be either “from my flesh,” i.e., while Job lives, in this life or possibly in a postmortem experience; or “apart from my flesh,” possibly in a disembodied state (text note). Since the book does touch on the idea of resurrection in ch. 14, it seems likely that when death is spoken of in v. 26, resurrection is in view, and the translation should be “in” my flesh. What is certain is that Job believes he has a Redeemer who loves him and for whom his heart yearns (v. 27). The whole passage is strongly evocative of every sinner’s need for the one mediator who is both God and man (1 Tim. 2:5, 6).

Job emphatically anticipates personally witnessing this vindication, whether with the eyes of a resurrected body or with spiritual perception.

**My heart faints within me.** In his anguished condition, Job yearns even more intensely for the resolution of his perplexity.

In the light of the eternal destiny that awaits them, Job solemnly cautions his friends not to misjudge his situation or continue their pursuit of him (see v. 22). His warning is similar to that of Christ in Matt. 7:1–5.

**The root of the matter.** He is the cause of his own misfortunes.

**the sword.** The instrument of divine justice., 29

This speech is Zophar’s final contribution to the exchange of views between the friends and Job. It consists of another eloquent statement of the fate of the wicked. In it, Zophar expresses the truth of the moral governance of the world by God but fails to make a correct application of it.

Feeling personally insulted by Job’s words, Zophar again sets out the view that the joys of the wicked soon vanish. A godless individual will quickly perish, particularly because of his inflated self-esteem (vv. 5–7).

**20:2 my thoughts.** The term applies to anxious or disquieting thoughts. Zophar has been upset by Job’s vigorous rebuttal of the counsel extended to him.

**my haste within me.** Job’s closing words in 19:28, 29, threatening impending judgment, have not been lost on Zophar.
Job’s claim was that God had closed the friends’ hearts to understanding (17:4), a thought Zophar indignantly counters.
The allusion seems to be to the tower of Babel (see Gen. 11:4) and implies that Job is as arrogant a sinner as there has ever been (see v. 4).

verse_quote: His children will seek the favor of the poor.
note:
Portrays the children as having to beg from the very people their father had oppressed, or, less probably, presents them as having to make restitution to the poor.

**give back his wealth.** Repeatedly Zophar mentions the wealth of the wicked (also vv. 15, 18, 21, 22, 26), insinuating that Job acquired his former wealth dishonestly.

–**19** Zophar argues that even though a wicked man displays an insatiable relish for ill-gotten wealth, it will poison him, and he will be forced to relinquish it. He will have to disgorge what he had taken such pains to obtain (see Eccl. 2:18–23).
A coarse expression of the operation of retributive justice: what a man swallows poisons him and has to be vomited up.
“Curds” refers to curdled milk, a much-appreciated form of yogurt. The sinner will be deprived of the delicacies he expended so much effort to acquire.
Misuse of wealth and power to oppress the less fortunate is characteristic of the ruthlessness of those who cherish material prosperity (see Amos 2:6–8; 8:4–6).

–**29** Zophar emphasizes that God does not let a wicked person escape the consequences of his actions. Divine wrath will change their ease and prosperity into distress and calamity.

**20:20 knew no contentment.** Zophar argues that the wicked man (implicitly, Job) always craves more and will consume anything he can.

No matter how hard the wicked man tries to escape punishment, even the heavens and the earth will give evidence against him, a clear reference to Job’s wish in 16:18–21. Zophar is convinced that the miserable turn Job’s circumstances have taken is a sure indicator that he is no longer in God’s favor.
Lit. “produce.” It is possible that the word rendered “possessions” should be understood as “a flood”; that is, “a flood carries away his house.” In either case, the picture is that of a total loss.

verse_quote: This is the wicked man’s portion from God.
note: What Zophar teaches will ultimately come to pass, but, sadly, he has no word to say about God’s mercy. Even in his earlier speech in 11:13–20, where he called on Job to change his ways, there was no mention of mercy. According to Zophar, people receive God’s blessing only by earning it.

Job’s sixth speech closes this second cycle with a firm rejection of the friends’ arguments that the wicked always suffer in this life. Unlike his other responses, Job makes no appeal to God. Throughout the chapter he uses plural forms when referring to his friends (but see v. 3 note), though he does rebut Zophar’s allegations from the previous chapter. Note how he alludes to their very words: cf. 20:11 with 21:7; 8:19 with 21:8; 18:5 with 21:17; 5:4 and 20:10 with 21:19; and 20:5–7 with 21:28–30.

After another plea that his friends actually listen to what he has to say rather than just repeating their preconceived, simplistic notions (vv. 2, 3), Job calls on them to “look” (v. 5) at his misery. Surely they should be compassionate about one in such a piteous state.

**21:2 let this be your comfort.** The solace they offer him. They should at least extend to him the consolation and support he would receive if they took seriously what he was saying. Note the similar phrase in v. 34, bracketing this speech.

Unlike the other verbs in the chapter, this is singular, addressed to Zophar, and ironically conceding to him the right to continue his bitter attacks if only he will first actually listen to what Job has to say about his situation.

verse_quote: Look at me and be appalled, and lay your hand over your mouth.
note: If they have any compassion, Job says, they will stop accusing him and lying about him.
Job is probably referring to the condition he is in. If he shudders at it, should not his friends shudder with him?

Job insists that the available evidence about the prosperity and longevity of the wicked refutes Zophar’s argument that they die young (e.g., in 20:11). It is simply not the case that they always receive their recompense in this life. The wicked flourish (vv. 7–13) even while they defy God (vv. 14–16).

**21:7 Why do the wicked live.** Job admits that he is perplexed by the ease and grandeur enjoyed by the wicked. He has no answer (see Ps. 73:3). The counselors assume that they know exactly what is going on (see John 9:41).
Bildad earlier claimed that they would have no offspring (18:19).

verse_quote: no rod of God is upon them.
note: God does not chastise them but allows them to prosper.
The prosperity of the wicked continues even though they openly flout God., 15
In a series of rhetorical questions, Job points out that it is not the case that “the light of the wicked is put out,” as Bildad claimed (18:5).

The prosperity of the wicked cannot be evaded by saying that God will punish their children. It has already been claimed they will have no children, and once they die, they are unaffected by the suffering of their offspring. It is the wicked themselves who should experience divine punishment., 20

Job picks up earlier assertions of Eliphaz (see 4:18; 15:15). Job’s high view of God only makes his problem more perplexing. He acknowledges the inscrutability of God’s action when one person dies young and prosperous while another lives long in deprivation and adversity. Though all lives end in death, their spiritual condition cannot be judged by external circumstances.

Job anticipates that his counselors will try to discount his argument by asking where wicked, wealthy people have lived. He inquires in return if they have quizzed the widely traveled. Is he accusing his friends of living in ivory towers, out of touch with what is obvious to others? It is not difficult to find instances of evil men enjoying relief from calamity and popularity and thus not being openly denounced.
Job has found no satisfactory explanation of his condition in what his friends have said to comfort him. All their arguments are deceptive and unreliable.

In this final cycle of speeches, Bildad’s contribution is brief (25:1–6), and Zophar does not speak at all. Although attempts have been made to find the missing speech in ch. 26, it is more probable that the intention is to show the exhaustion of the friends. In these chapters they openly accuse him of sin (22:5–9; 25:5, 6), of which he needs to repent (22:21–23). But Job cannot do what they urge and maintains his integrity because he does not know of any sin to be confessed.

**22:1–30** Eliphaz begins the third cycle of speeches (22:1–26:14), listing Job’s sins and calling on him to repent.

Eliphaz does two things: he emphasizes the transcendence of God (vv. 2–4) and lists the many sins of which he considers Job to be guilty (vv. 5–9). His sin explains his situation; he is being appropriately punished.

**22:2, 3** Eliphaz reacts to Job’s statement that God allows wickedness to go unpunished, and he also says that human uprightness adds nothing to God. Eliphaz espouses such a transcendent view of God that it pictures Him as unconcerned with the details of life on earth (see vv. 12–14) and with Job’s situation. It is therefore pointless for Job to be so obsessed with vindication. His suffering is what he deserves.

**22:3** The sense may be, “Would it please God if you were vindicated?” Since all comes from God, we have nothing to give back to Him that is not His in the first place.

Eliphaz reaches the conclusion Zophar and Bildad have already expressed—that Job’s sins are endless. In the light of the following line, “your evil” refers to Job’s wrongdoing rather than to the misery he is enduring.

Here is a direct personal attack on Job for specific sins, especially social sins against the poor and widows. Later Job will emphasize his social righteousness (chs. 29; 31). Eliphaz has no evidence to substantiate these allegations against Job. He is simply arguing back from the intensity of Job’s suffering.

Eliphaz makes no secret of his conviction that Job had adopted the lifestyle of the wicked before disaster struck him (v. 15).

**22:12–14** Eliphaz attacks Job’s complaint that God is absent (13:24). It is not unnatural for Job, in the midst of suffering, to complain that God is either too observant and intrusive to leave him alone (7:17–19; 10:8; 16:9) or too far away. It looks as though Eliphaz attributes words to Job twice—vv. 13, 14 (clearly so), and perhaps also v. 17 or vv. 17, 18—and counters both of them.

Once more Eliphaz presents the fate of the wicked in simplistic terms. They die prematurely (v. 16). Despite their rejection of God (v. 17; see 21:14, 15), He has abundantly blessed them (v. 18).

**22:15 old way.** That of living in defiance of God.

verse_quote: the counsel of the wicked is far from me.
note: Eliphaz rejects Job’s claim that God prospers the wicked. It is best to understand Eliphaz as reflecting what Job said but claiming that the prosperity of the wicked is followed by disaster. Eliphaz employs Job’s phrase from 21:16 to describe Job’s own position.
The rejoicing of the righteous is evidence of the fall of the wicked. “Mock” recalls divine mockery in Ps. 2:4.

In his final entreaty to Job, Eliphaz sets out to an even greater extent the blessings he will enjoy if only he repents (vv. 21–23). He should also renounce claims to his wealth as being his own (v. 24). Eliphaz remains convinced that Job is guilty (v. 30), and his advice is grounded on that assumption. Consequently, what he says fails to comprehend the nature of Job’s situation.
The words are ironic. It is Eliphaz himself who will be delivered through Job’s intercession (42:7–9).

Job does not take up what Eliphaz has just said until ch. 31. Instead he gives vent to matters immediately weighing upon him. He wants to present his case directly to God (23:1–7), but God will not grant him a hearing and is acting unfairly toward him (23:8–17). Furthermore, there are many aspects of divine implementation of justice that leave Job confused and mystified (ch. 24).

**23:1–12** Job’s thoughts vacillate. In ch. 9 he doubts God would give him a hearing. In ch. 13 he is convinced he will get a hearing and be vindicated. In 17:1 he is convinced that only death awaits him but also that his counselors will not triumph, and that he will be vindicated (17:10–16). That conviction reaches its zenith in 19:25–27, and from then on he never again doubts it, as these verses and especially ch. 31 prove.

Job probably has his friends in view. What they have said has not connected with his situation or relieved his distress.

**my hand is heavy.** The idiom denotes weariness and inability to act. His grievous condition has drained Job of strength.

Refers to where God acts as judge.

**23:3–9** Job has not been successful in ascertaining why God has afflicted him (see 9:10, 11).
If he were to receive an audience with the Lord, Job would set out why he considers himself innocent of any offense that warrants the imposition of such suffering.
“Contend” implies engaging in legal argument (9:3 note). Job believes that the arguments he could present would be so convincing that God would declare him innocent.

Though Job knows God is present, he is unable to sense His presence (vv. 8, 9). He is now certain he will get a hearing (v. 10) that will vindicate him because he has obeyed God’s Word.

**23:8** Job’s God is invisible, but He has an all-seeing eye (v. 10). The four directions of movement in vv. 8, 9 are all-inclusive, possibly representing east, west, north, and south, respectively.

For “tried,” see “test” (7:18). Job confidently expects to come out of the process of divine trial completely vindicated. Job has in view not God’s using this experience to advance his spirituality, but the expectation that when he is granted a hearing, divine scrutiny of his conduct will endorse his claim that he has done nothing to merit his suffering. Chapter 42 shows that the outcome is not quite as Job anticipates here.
Job responds to Eliphaz’s injunction to “agree with God” in 22:21 by insisting that he has always lived in harmony with God’s ways and treasured God’s Word., 12

Lit. “one,” perhaps signifying “unique.” Job returns to asserting his confidence in God’s sovereign control. Even though he does not understand, he affirms that God will surely accomplish what He desires for Job. This consideration seems to undermine his confidence in appearing in court before Him (v. 15)., 14

Job’s friends think they understand all about God and His ways and therefore are able to predict what God will do. Job realizes that there is much he does not understand about God, and he is therefore daunted and dismayed before Him.

Despite the ordeal he is undergoing, his lack of comprehension of what is occurring, and his overwhelming dread before God, Job considers that he has no option but to continue to plead to be heard and vindicated.

Job has not yet learned the important lesson that justice in this world does not operate mechanically but according to the will of God. If it were not so, the human race would have perished long ago. This chapter alternates between descriptions of the fortunate wicked and the sufferings of their victims, with emphasis on the sufferings. Job wants the wicked to be judged so that those who know God will see it and know that God is just. The chapter shows Job’s hatred of wickedness.

**24:1–12** Job reverts to his earlier theme that the unrighteous prosper (ch. 21) while God does not intervene in judgment. Job lists the crimes of which the wicked are guilty (vv. 2–4, 9, 13–17, 21) and here particularly details the deprivation and injustice arising from their exploitation of the poor and defenseless (vv. 5–12).

**24:1 see his days.** The days in view are the times when God intervenes in the flow of human history to judge wickedness and ensure that justice prevails in human affairs. Job complains that this does not happen immediately, even though the wicked sin flagrantly. The prophets later talk about “the day of the LORD” as a future time of judgment on the nations and blessing of His people (see Joel 2:1, 2; Amos 5:18–20), when God will openly display His control of affairs.

verse_quote: God charges no one with wrong.
note: Job’s most sweeping allegation against God—that He is not concerned about administering justice (9:24 note; cf. Ps. 50:21; Lam. 3:34–36).

Job focuses on the misconduct of the wicked, singling out murder (v. 14), adultery (v. 15) and theft (v. 16). Throughout he emphasizes the covert nature of their activities, as the wicked operate in darkness and shun both the light of day and the light of truth.

Often considered an unannounced quotation from the counselors since the views expressed here seem more consistent with their position than Job’s (24:18 note). Others think the whole chapter is an attempt by early editors to make Job sound more orthodox. But Job may have a reason for seeming to adopt the counselors’ stance.

**24:18 You say.** A translator’s addition to clarify that vv. 18–24 are the words of the counselors. Job is expostulating against his friends’ inability to see what is so obviously happening: the imposition of divine judgment is delayed. The friends continue to hold that the wicked are carried away as swiftly as something floating on a stream or perhaps like a bubble or eddy on the surface of the stream.

These seem to be Job’s words, emphasizing the wrongdoing of the wicked (v. 21) but claiming that God prolongs their lives and grants them prosperity. Still, Job argues, their thriving condition lasts only for a little. God deals with them not immediately but gradually.

These verses must be connected with v. 1 in order to understand the point of the chapter. Job is trying to show that though the wicked are punished, this punishment takes place little by little, while the righteous want to see justice meted out completely and immediately. Job’s thought anticipates the “day of the LORD” doctrine of the prophets, which looks for the final judgment day. Conversely, Job claims to be suffering wrongfully, yet God will not hear him because He has not set times for judgment. Even so, Job holds to God’s justice and expects vindication eventually, though he would rather it come more speedily., 24
This is a veiled threat to his friends. If God’s justice does not operate with immediate effect, then they too must be fearful and not presume (see 19:29; 27:7–13).
Bildad makes no new argument but repeats what has already been said about God’s dominion and power (vv. 2, 3) and about His moral purity, which is in marked contrast to mankind’s (vv. 4–6).

verse_quote: be in the right before God.
note: Human impurity is a given, but missing here is a hint of grace. Paul, who developed the doctrine of the total depravity of man in Romans, did so as a background for God’s marvelous grace. Bildad does not think in terms of grace.

Bildad risks overstating the depth of human worthlessness because he has a pessimistic view of man (see Eliphaz in 15:14–16). The doctrine of total depravity is not pessimistic. Even in their sinful condition, human beings retain the image of God, giving each person dignity and value. Furthermore, Bildad’s sweeping generalization does not begin to connect with the specifics of Job’s circumstances.

This chapter falls into two distinct parts: vv. 1–4 and vv. 5–14, which has led some to say that only the opening verses are Job’s while the rest of the chapter is Bildad’s, or is a third speech by Zophar, thus identifying three speeches of the counselors in the third cycle.
“You” in these verses is singular; Job explicitly addresses Bildad and scathingly mocks his ineffective attempts to strengthen or enlighten him regarding what is happening., 3
Job suggests that Bildad’s words have some source other than God.

These verses celebrate God’s omnipotence. They are not unlike Job’s words in 9:5–10 and need not be assigned, as they sometimes are, to one of the counselors. Job will not take second place to his friends when it comes to acknowledging God’s sovereign dominion. His problem concerns the equity of God’s actions.

**26:5 The dead.** Lit. “the Rephaim,” a term variously used but here referring to the shadowy existence of those who have departed this life (see Is. 14:9).

**26:5, 6** Unlike the Canaanite gods, who each have a restricted domain of power, the true God controls even Sheol (Prov. 15:11), the supposed domain of Mot, the god of death.

**26:6 Abaddon.** “The place of destruction” (see 28:22; 31:12), another term for Sheol.

Job’s purpose here is not to teach the science of space or weather but to glorify God through the mysteries of His work in nature. The whole created realm continues in existence solely by God’s sustaining power., 8

Another word, “throne,” is spelled the same way in Hebrew (text note); if it is applied here, it would indicate God’s refusal to disclose all that is decided in His heavenly council chamber. The context favors a description of divine control of the natural realm.
Possibly a reference to the mountains, which often reach into the clouds and appear to support the sky.

God rules the supposed dominion of Yam, the Canaanite god of the sea. Jesus Christ showed He is the true God of His people when He calmed the sea in Matt. 8:23–27.

**Rahab.** A mythical Canaanite monster of the deep, similar to Leviathan, capable of wreaking havoc. This poetic imagery enriches the concept of God’s great power over the boisterous sea (Ps. 89:9, 10).

A further description of the Canaanite sea god (v. 12 note). Every conceivable power is under the control of the one true God. This will be finally demonstrated when Satan is overwhelmed by the power of Christ (John 12:31; Rev. 20:7–10).

Job is aware that such phenomena only hint at the full extent of divine power. Since even there, God’s ways lie beyond human comprehension, Job’s friends are presumptuous to suppose that they can unerringly interpret God’s dealings with him.

The structure of the book of Job at this point is much disputed. There are two issues: How ch. 28 relates to the surrounding chapters and whether a third speech by Zophar is found in ch. 27. Given that the author is meticulous elsewhere in noting who is speaking, he is unlikely to have been negligent here. There are two clear introductory formulas in 27:1 and 29:1, which bracket chs. 27; 28 and designate them as Job’s speech. (For further details, see notes on these verses and the introduction to ch. 28.) When Job becomes aware that his friends are not going to speak again, he takes the opportunity to conclude their interchange by reasserting his innocence (ch. 27) and by setting the whole debate in a broader context, the need for true fear of the Lord (ch. 28). Thus, along with ch. 3, where Job also speaks, these chapters function as brackets to enclose Job’s disputation with the three counselors.

**27:1–23** Job rounds off the discussion by insisting once more on his innocence (vv. 2–6) and by describing the destiny of the wicked (vv. 7–23). Using words similar to those employed by his friends, Job calls the fate of the godless to fall on them. Since his expression resembles that of his friends, attempts have been made to reconstruct a third speech of Zophar from vv. 7–23. That misses the point that Job likewise accepts a simplistic version of retribution theology. It also fails to account for the language of vv. 11, 12.

**27:1 Job again took up his discourse.** While this indicates continuity of speaker from ch. 26, it also suggests that some interval has occurred from the preceding speech (see 29:1). Note the repeated use of a similar formula to introduce various distinct speeches of Balaam in Num. 23; 24.

These verses are directed at the counselors (“you” is plural in v. 5). With a most solemn oath founded on God’s existence, Job denies their false accusations and at the same time asserts his integrity. As long as he lives, Job will not admit to wrongdoing in the way his friends are urging (v. 5). He has no qualms of conscience regarding his conduct (v. 6).

**27:2 God ... Almighty.** Job does not deny the existence or power of God, but the qualifying clauses he adds to the divine name express his frustration and grievance regarding the justice of God’s dealings with him. For “soul bitter,” see note on 3:20.

Job poses four rhetorical questions that emphasize the hopeless condition of the godless. He calls for his friends who have falsely accused him of being wicked to share their fate.

**27:7–10** Curses like these are found in the Psalms (Pss. 109:6–15; 139:19–22). See Introduction to Psalms.

The pronouns are plural and can be accounted for only by supposing Job is speaking to his friends. They do not fit in with attempts to identify here a speech of one of his friends. Rather, Job claims to be able to instruct them regarding “the hand of God,” that is, how God will intervene in judgment., 12

Job turns to discuss the fate of the wicked, a topic addressed at length by his counselors. His comments show that he understands it as well as they do. He has never disputed the ultimate fate of the wicked; it is their immediate punishment that he denies, in contrast to Zophar’s assertion (20:5; 21:7). But Job makes the counselors and not himself the implied objects of the destiny described.
A reference to death in military conflict.

verse_quote: like a moth’s, like a booth.
note: Though the wicked think they erect solid structures as homes, those homes will in fact prove to be insubstantial and transient.

Gestures of derision at the helpless state of the wicked. While vv. 22, 23 may extend the description of the east wind, as the ESV margin notes, the subject may well be God so that these lines directly detail His scornful dismissal of the wicked.

A different type of wisdom literature is presented in ch. 28, a kind of standard wisdom like that found in the book of Proverbs. The lack of an introductory formula indicating the speaker might indicate that this is an insertion by the author of Job, reflecting on the lack of wisdom displayed so far in the dialogue. However, the text does not indicate a change of speaker from ch. 27, so it is probable that ch. 28 is spoken by Job. After his extended yet unsatisfactory dialogue with his friends, he experiences a period of relative tranquility in which he muses on how to find wisdom—the capacity to make right decisions and cope with life. Job’s reflective mood continues into ch. 29, where he recalls his past happiness before he is again overwhelmed by his present distress (chs. 30; 31).

The subject of the poem is the elusiveness and surpassing value of true wisdom. It may be analyzed as having three stanzas (vv. 1–12, 13–20, 21–28), though the refrain in vv. 12, 20 is transitional and may also be read with what follows. The refrain asks the key question, “Where shall wisdom be found?” and the answer is provided in the concluding verse of the poem (v. 28).

**28:1–12** Job reflects on the great skill and tenacity with which mankind has gathered hidden treasures from the depths of the earth. However, such technological exploits must be surpassed to acquire wisdom.
The darkness of underground caverns can be dispelled by lamps or torches, but this might be an implied contrast with other forms of darkness—intellectual and spiritual.
Envisions miners being lowered down shafts using ropes.

Likely not a reference to volcanic activity. It is a contrast between fields above ground and the upheaval and rubble hidden in the mine workings below ground. It is like debris from a burned building.
Or “lapis lazuli” (text note). Both are highly prized, blue gemstones.
Mining is a human achievement that sets mankind apart from animals., 8
This transitional verse emphasizes that technological know-how is incapable of providing spiritual insight.

The principal theme of this stanza is the value of true wisdom, even though weak, mortal man fails to appreciate its worth (v. 13). It cannot be found by exploring ocean depths (v. 14) or by trading in the marketplace. Wisdom is not for sale.
The closing stanza of the poem contrasts the inability of the created realm to find wisdom with God’s complete grasp of it.
The place of destruction (26:6 note). Abaddon and Death are personified; they have only heard a rumor (from those who have died?) that wisdom exists.

–**27 God understands the way to it.** As creator, God alone knows where true wisdom is to be found. There is nothing hidden from His scrutiny (v. 24). From the very beginning, He established how mankind should live.

Mankind can acquire wisdom only from God, and He has not concealed it. It is obtained through obedience to His revealed will (Deut. 4:5, 6; Prov. 8:4–9; 9:10). For the NT application, see Col. 2:2, 3 and Eph. 3:8–10.

**fear of the Lord.** This key phrase of wisdom teaching (see Ps. 111:10; Prov. 1:7) embodies respectful acknowledgment of God’s existence, authority, and standards. “Lord” here is Adonai, “sovereign master” (the sole occurrence of the term in Job), and not Yahweh, the covenant name of God. This advice has universal applicability.

**turn away from evil.** Includes both a positive attitude toward God and avoidance of all that is contrary to His commands (see Prov. 3:7). If Job is here reproaching his friends for failing to show proper respect for God, there is irony in the fact that he is also condemning himself by his self-righteous presumption in challenging God, which becomes even more evident in the following chapters.

There now follow three monologues. In the first of these, Job summarizes his case against God (chs. 29–31). Then Elihu intervenes to object to the way in which God’s justice has been inadequately defended and presents his perspective on the situation (chs. 32–37). Finally, God Himself speaks to resolve the situation (chs. 38–41).

**29:1–31:40** Job addresses God in the form of a case presented in court. He first establishes the loss he has suffered as he looks back poignantly to the affluence and respect he previously enjoyed (ch. 29). In ch. 30 he expresses his gloom and dismay at his loss, especially the loss of friendship with God. In ch. 31 he defends himself and delivers a final oath of innocence, which he feels should settle matters once and for all in his favor.

**29:1–25** Job sues for restitution of what he has lost. In effect, this chapter expands on his affirmation of his previous circumstances, “I was at ease” (16:12).

**29:1 took up his discourse.** This does not necessarily indicate a change of speaker but may indicate a new division or the passage of time before the start of a new speech (27:1 note).

Job bemoans the loss of God’s favor. He nostalgically yearns for what he formerly enjoyed (note the repetition of “when”).

**29:2 months of old.** Job’s prosperity obviously extended over a considerable period of time.
Light symbolizes God’s blessing. This illustration is based on a lamp dispelling the gloom inside a tent.

Lit. “in days of my autumn/winter.” The point of the metaphor is unclear. It may well indicate the time when Job was enjoying the produce of his labor and fellowship with God. That, of course, was precisely what Satan pointed to as the reason for Job’s piety.

**the friendship of God.** Lit. “the council of God.” Pictured is a scene of familiarity such as is found in Gen. 18, particularly vv. 17–19. Job always viewed God as the source of his good fortune, the root of which was his intimate relationship with God.

verse_quote: my children were all around me.
note: Job recalls the happiness of family life while his children were still alive and gathered around him.
Choice luxury goods. Job enjoyed an abundant lifestyle.

Job was once a figure of standing, respected throughout the community. When he spoke, his sage advice caused others to fall silent (vv. 9, 10).

**29:7 the gate of the city.** Where the commercial and legal business of the community was conducted in the ancient Near East.

Job recalls the noble reputation he had built as a practitioner of what the NT calls “pure and undefiled” religion (cf. vv. 12–16 with James 1:27). He was respected not just because he was rich, powerful, and wise, but because of his compassionate intervention on behalf of the vulnerable (contrary to Eliphaz’s allegations in 22:6–9).

verse_quote: righteousness ... clothed me ... justice was like a robe and a turban.
note: This verse is the center point of the chapter, an emphatic assertion of Job’s call for vindication.

verse_quote: broke the fangs of the unrighteous.
note: Those who preyed on others in dire need are compared to wild animals. The action Job took rendered them incapable of inflicting injury.

In light of his past deeds, Job had expected to be vigorous in the later years of his life. This reflects the fact that he too accepted a simplistic version of retribution theology.

**29:18 in my nest.** A picture of security and absence of worries. In such circumstances, Job had expected to enjoy continuing respect and to die in peace.
The image changes to that of a tree, nourished by its access to water (see Ps. 1:3; Jer. 17:8).
Job remembers his former dignity and honor. The advice he gave was eagerly awaited and readily accepted.
Job had merely to look at those who were uncertain, and they were encouraged.

“But” and “And now” (30:1, 9, 16) move the time frame from the past of ch. 29 to the present. Here, point for point, Job laments how the blessings he enjoyed were taken away from him. In ch. 29 he dealt with honor from man, blessings from God, and his own benevolent deeds. This chapter describes how all that has been reversed.

**30:1–8** Job describes those who ridicule and insult him. Previously, the young men of the community had treated him with esteem (29:8). Now, contrary to ancient deference to elders, they display utter disrespect by mocking him. Moreover, Job’s shame is intensified because those who mock him are not just young but the offspring of disreputable scoundrels.

The group Job describes are those eking out an existence in marginal land on the edge of the community, such as runaway slaves or absconding criminals. They have to eat the poorest of food and live without permanent homes or adequate shelter. These verses are a good example of the discursive style of the poet.

Job bewails the dishonor he receives from these criminals (see 29:7–10, 21–25). Even such social misfits and outcasts consider themselves more fortunate than Job and are not slow to insult him as he sits on the city rubbish heap.
Likely an analogy of a loosened bowstring, which is therefore incapable of being used effectively (cf. 29:20). Alternatively, the cord may be what once held up his tent (see 29:4).

Job is no longer respected or safe in the situation to which God has brought him (cf. 29:7–11).

**30:12 cast up.** The image is that of an army conducting a siege. See “wide breach” (v. 14).

Job is physically in pain (vv. 16–19), but worse still is the spiritual trauma arising from the recognition that it is God who is subjecting him to this treatment and refusing to pay attention to his pleas for relief (vv. 20, 21). Cf. 29:2–6, 18–20.
The Septuagint reads, “He seizes my garment.” Job is talking again as if God is his enemy.
Symbols of abject humiliation. Job, however, may have been literally covered by them (2:8 and note).
“You” is singular, referring to God. Job accuses God of abusing His position by ignoring Job’s petition and need.

See 29:11–17. Job again describes his intense physical and emotional pain. Though he comforted others in the past (v. 25), he now receives no assistance from his friends. They forget his former kindness. As a conse­quence, he is drained physically and emotionally (vv. 27–31).

verse_quote: darkened, but not by the sun.
note: His affliction has caused his skin to darken (see v. 30).
In his agony, Job has uttered sounds like the wailing of jackals or the groans of ostriches (see Is. 13:21; Mic. 1:8).
Job’s life is no longer regaled by music. He hears only the shrill tones of mourning and weeping.

Uppermost in Job’s mind is the false accusation that he is a man of exceptional wickedness, suffering no more than what he deserves. To counter this allegation, Job employs a legal procedure that is common in his day: he calls on the gods to impose a curse on him if he is guilty of the charges. So Job solemnly rebuts various forms of misconduct and sets out the sanctions God should impose on him if he is lying. Although this is a protestation of innocence, it is not the self-righteousness of the Pharisee in Luke 18:11, 12. Like the psalmist, Job is the victim of false accusation, so vindication has become his passion.

Job’s thinking is governed by a simplistic principle of retribution. If he has acted sinfully, then he will accept that he has been justly cursed. However, the converse proposition is implicit: since he has not acted inappropriately, he should be acquitted and reinstated in divine blessing. Job’s logic is irrefutable. Like his friends, however, he has illegitimately extended the scope of the retribution principle and is attempting to use it to force God into acting as he demands. It is this coercive approach to God that Job has later to repent of (see 42:6).

**31:1–4** Job declares that he had determined not to sin with his eyes (1 John 2:16). God would have been aware of such transgression (v. 4) and would justly punish it (v. 3). However, Job may be speaking of more than ordinary lust. He may have in view worship of the fertility goddesses so popular in OT times. The word translated “virgin” (v. 1) is used of the goddess of fertility in Canaanite writings. She was a kind of Venus and was called the “maiden Anat” in the city of Ugarit.

Job clears himself of avarice in his business dealings. In v. 6 he declares his “integrity,” not an assertion of sinless perfection but of genuine probity and honesty. He therefore does not shrink from being weighed in God’s balances.
The penalty Job sees as appropriate is a curse of reversal and frustration (see Deut. 28:30–41).
Job clears himself of adultery. If he had violated another man’s wife, then the curse should have come on his own marriage.
Grinding grain is viewed as the most menial of tasks in this era.
Job acknowledges that adultery is so serious an offense that it merits the sanctions of human and divine justice., 12
Job clears himself of injustice with respect to his servants. If he had rejected their claims for fair treatment, he would have no grounds for complaining about God’s treatment of him.
Job disregards the class structures of his society and recognizes the basic equality before God of master and servant alike (see Prov. 22:2).
Job clears himself of neglect of the needy and abuse of the helpless (see 29:12–17).

Probably not a threat to strike them but rather a gesture employed in taking an oath. Job had not given false evidence to deprive them of their rights even though his “help” was “in the gate”; that is, even though he knew of some who would support him in whatever action he took in public affairs (see 29:7).
The curse that should befall him would render him incapable of raising his hand to subscribe to a false oath (v. 21).
Job avoided social injustice because he dreaded the penalty God would rightly impose on it.

Job clears himself of idolatry with regard to gold or the gods.

**31:24, 25** Though Job had enjoyed considerable affluence (1:3), he had not made it his source of confidence for living., 25
Worship of the sun and the moon was widely practiced throughout the ancient Near East.
Kissing one’s hand was a recognized devotional gesture in the ancient Near East (see 1 Kin. 19:18; Hos. 13:2).

The structure of Job’s thought is somewhat complex here. Verses 29–34 and 38–40 continue to present in conditional form the behavior he has avoided. On the basis of his assertion of innocence, he breaks off in the central verses (vv. 35–37) to express his basic demand. He wants a hearing with God. If he has been responsible for such misconduct, then, in terms of his simplistic retribution theology, he ought to be indicted and punished; if not, he deserves his day in court to clear his name. Job appears supremely confident that he would be successful in achieving such an outcome.

**31:29–34** Job clears himself of hatred, selfishness, and hypocrisy. He had not harbored malevolent attitudes toward those who opposed him (see Ps. 35:13, 14; Matt. 5:43–47).
Members of Job’s household looked out for those who would benefit from Job’s benevolence, including travelers passing by (v. 32).
“As mankind does,” or possibly “as Adam did” (text note), in which case the reference is to Gen. 3:8.
Behavior Job has avoided. He has not covered up his transgressions or avoided people out of fear of public opinion.

The climax. The repeated “Oh, that I had” embody Job’s perception that having his case heard will lead to his vindication. He views God as his adversary and attaches his binding signature to his challenge to God to issue specific charges against him.
Job would proudly wear God’s written indictment, a sign that he considers any accusations against him easily refutable.
Job has already expressed confidence that God would accept him if he had an opportunity to present his case (13:14–16). In the end, this is possible only through grace.

Job again denies that he had ever abused his position as a wealthy landowner. He had not misappropriated the crops of his tenants or imposed on them unreasonable conditions. If he had, then his fields would have rightly become unfruitful and overgrown with weeds.

verse_quote: The words of Job are ended.
note: Job closes his case. The rest is now up to the Judge. Job apparently thinks that his protestation of innocence will force God to act, but there is no immediate response. God neither affirms Job’s innocence nor imposes any penalty for perjury. Instead, the way is open for Elihu’s intervention in the following six chapters.

These chapters present the second monologue, that of the young man Elihu, who, unlike the others, has a Hebrew name (32:2). Commentators do not know what to make of him. Many dismiss him as wordy, self-important, and irrelevant, and say he merely reiterates what has already been said. Indeed, some critics believe these chapters are additions to the original text, since Job makes no reply to Elihu, and he is ignored in the epilogue. Both views are defective. The author of Job gives Elihu a formal introduction (32:1–5) and accords six chapters to what he has to say. That is difficult to square with an easy rejection of his contribution. Furthermore, Elihu is not mentioned in the epilogue (ch. 42), not because he is irrelevant, but because he is not guilty of the same errors as the other three. Elihu’s critique centers on Job’s words uttered during the dispute. He quotes Job but does not accuse him of having lived a wicked life. He stresses an issue neglected by the three friends: the disciplinary and redemptive role of suffering. Eliphaz alone has touched on suffering as discipline (5:17).

**32:1–5** The narrator introduces Elihu’s four speeches on Job’s situation with an explanation for why Elihu injects himself into the debate.
