**32:1 righteous in his own eyes.** Job has stoutly insisted upon his innocence despite his suffering. Since the friends have been unable to induce Job to adopt their analysis of his situation, they view him as incorrigible and intransigent. There is no point in saying anything more to him.

The genealogy shows the narrator considers Elihu (his name means “He is my God”) a significant figure. Nothing is known about Barachel, but there was a Ram who was an ancestor of David (Ruth 4:19; 1 Chr. 2:9, 25), and there was a Buz connected with Abraham (Gen. 22:21).

**burned with anger.** Elihu does not want to see God’s justice compromised, and he sees Job’s focus on his innocence as doing that very thing.

verse_quote: declared Job to be in the wrong.
note: According to ancient Jewish tradition, the original reading (“condemned Elohim”) was changed by pious convention to “condemned Job,” so as to avoid writing a blasphemous thought. Elihu’s anger with the friends seems to arise from their failure to establish that God is acting justly.
According to the conventions of the time, older men speak first.

Elihu’s introduction, including his reason for speaking, runs to 33:7. He appears to have a warmer personality than the counselors, who never called Job by his name (see 33:1, 31).

**32:6–10** Elihu first addresses all four who have spoken thus far. He deferentially explains why he is speaking despite his youth. God has given him something to say.

**32:6, 10, 17 my opinion.** Lit. “my knowledge.” Elihu claims more than an alternative viewpoint. He has definite, God-imparted insight into the situation and so can contribute at a different level. Moreover, he is sure that he will be able to convince the others that his approach is right., 10, 17

verse_quote: the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty.
note: These phrases are in apposition in the parallelism and have the same reference. Elihu claims that the experience and observation of age don’t really impart knowledge (v. 9) but insight from God, which is accessible also to the young. “The spirit in a man” may here refer to the Holy Spirit as the source of wisdom (see Gen. 41:38; Ex. 31:3).

Elihu next focuses on the three counselors. He listened to their addresses, but they failed to convince Job that he was in the wrong (v. 12).

**32:11 you searched out what to say.** Possibly the earlier rounds of speeches extended over days with the participants using the gaps to develop more effective arguments.
The friends could not rightly claim to possess wisdom beyond what God has revealed.
Elihu claims he is going to follow a different line of argument in answering Job.

Elihu no longer addresses the counselors, whom he refers to as “they” (v. 15). Instead he engages in a soliloquy that the others, especially Job, are intended to overhear. Elihu is mainly concerned with establishing his right to speak.

Elihu’s speeches are longer than the combined addresses of any one of the three friends.

**32:18–20 the spirit within me.** Probably Elihu’s inner being. He is ready to burst because there is so much he is eager to say. A wineskin required a vent so that the gases produced by the fermenting wine could escape without rupturing the wineskin.
Since Elihu disagrees with both Job and the friends, he will not favor either side in the dispute.

Elihu turns to address Job directly and pleads that Job listen to him.

**33:1 hear ... listen.** Elihu has perceived that the counselors were not listening to Job and that Job himself is not in a frame of mind to listen to anyone. Hence Elihu’s repeated injunctions to listen (33:1, 31, 33; 34:2, 10, 16, 34; 36:2, 10–12; 37:14).

**Job.** Elihu addresses Job by name three times (vv. 1, 31; 37:14) and names him seven other times (32:12, 14; 34:5, 7, 35, 36; 36:16). In contrast to the three counselors, who never mentioned Job’s name, Elihu’s approach displays a measure of empathy. However, he also appears condescending at times and overconfident in his ability.

verse_quote: The Spirit of God ... the breath of the Almighty.
note: See note on 32:8. Elihu goes beyond acknowledging that he too is a creature, dependent on God, to hinting that his message has a divine origin.

Elihu urges Job to respond to what he has to say, but Job never takes up his challenge, perhaps due to fatigue or to acceptance of the accuracy of what Elihu is saying. It is also possible that Job is resentful of Elihu’s intervention and dismissive of his contribution., 7

verse_quote: I am toward God as you are.
note: Lit. “I am as your mouth with respect to God.” Job had been looking for an intermediary (9:33 note); Elihu claims to fulfill that role, though he does so with a measure of modesty, acknowledging his frail origins. Even so, it is difficult to see how he thinks his presence might terrify Job (v. 7).

Elihu sets out the substance of his argument, and he begins by summarizing Job’s view of himself (v. 9) and of God’s attitude toward him (vv. 10, 11).

**33:8 your words.** Verbatim quotation was not the expected norm in ancient Near Eastern culture. Elihu’s summary fails to clarify that Job has never spoken of himself as absolutely sinless (see 7:21; 14:17). His claim of innocence concerns only the gross allegations made against him by the counselors (see 13:23).
A fair summary of Job’s utterance in 13:24, 27. He does feel that God is hostile toward him., 11

Elihu proceeds to correct Job’s perception of God. The counselors have already mentioned God’s transcendence, but Elihu approaches matters from a different perspective. Despite His transcendence, God does communicate with mankind through revelatory dreams (vv. 15–18) and through suffering (vv. 19–22).

**33:12 in this you are not right.** Job’s perception of his relationship with God is not well founded. Elihu does not conjure up errors in Job’s past life but focuses on what he has said in the interchange of views with his friends.

**God is greater than man.** Job has acknowledged the sovereignty and majesty of God. Therefore he is inconsistent when he alleges that God is doing wrong and when he demands that God explain himself. Elihu does not argue that greatness justifies injustice, but he hints that there may well be more behind Job’s experience than any human can appreciate.
That is, enter into a legal dispute with an individual (9:3 note). Job has argued that God is not responding to his arguments.
Contrary to Job’s perception, God has been speaking, but Job has not been listening, possibly because God has been speaking in ways Job did not anticipate.

The expression is equivalent to “reveals the truth to them.” God may send warnings in dreams so that an individual is kept alive.

**terrifies them with warnings.** This rendering follows the Septuagint. The Hebrew may be understood as “seals/confirms their instruction”; that is, dreams reinforce what men already know (see Ps. 16:7).
Elihu diagnoses Job’s fault as pride. Elihu also points out that God may speak to prevent wrongdoing as well as to pronounce sentence against sins.

Not the ordinary word for a sword, but one that signifies a weapon, particularly a missile such as a spear. “Perishing,” too, is unusual in that it signifies going or passing over, presumably to death. Some prefer to understand the line as embodying mythological references, identifying “sword” as a term for a “canal” or a “river” on the way to the realm of the dead.

Elihu adds another channel of divine communication with mankind—suffering—through which God gains an individual’s attention and compels him to think about final realities. “Rebuke” (v. 19) is part of a disciplinary process intended to bring reformation. Unlike the counselors, who saw no place for grace or mediation (5:1), Elihu knows God provides both. He also introduces the possibility of an angelic intermediary to plead with and for an individual.
Possibly a reference to angels who announce death (see Ps. 78:49).

Elihu pictures a hypothetical scene in which an angelic mediator (see Job’s earlier desire for such a figure, 9:32–35) intervenes on behalf of an individual, bringing to him divine truth and pleading with God to deliver him. This will be done on the basis of a “ransom” (v. 24), but it is not specified precisely what this will be.

**33:23 an angel.** The term basically means “messenger.” If here it refers to a superhuman being in general, the thought is not dissimilar to that of Gen. 48:16 (see also “the messenger of the covenant,” Mal. 3:1). Moreover, “one of the thousand,” or rather “one from a thousand,” points to the rarity, indeed the uniqueness, of the one in view here (see 9:3). He may well be identified with “the angel of the Lord.” In his intervention in the dispute between Job and his friends, Elihu himself faintly prefigures this unparalleled messenger.

**a mediator.** By introducing God’s redemptive purpose in Job’s suffering, Elihu substantially realigns the discussion.

**what is right for him.** The messenger’s declaration may be understood in two ways. It may consist of the true standard of right conduct (as in v. 27), which may be the means of bringing an individual to faith (see Gal. 3:19–24). Alternatively, “his uprightness” may be that of God Himself, which is perfectly disclosed by Christ as the consummating revelation of God (John 1:18). In either approach, the uprightness presented by the mediator exposes the inadequacy of mere human righteousness and points to the need for God’s merciful provision of what is lacking., 24

–**28** The outcome of the angelic mediation is that the sufferer is restored to physical health. This is accompanied by renewed spiritual vitality evidenced by prayer (of repentance, see v. 27) to God and restoration of a right standing before God (v. 26). “Sees his face” (v. 26) denotes a familiar relationship. The restored individual then witnesses to the gracious treatment he has received from God (v. 27, 28). “Look upon the light” refers to enjoyment of life (see v. 30).

verse_quote: he restores to man his righteousness.
note: This is the culmination of the gracious provision of a ransom appropriated through a prayer of confession. Divine acceptance of the repentant sinner leads to full restoration. As with “his uprightness” in 33:23, in “his righteousness” the personal pronoun may refer to the individual or to God. If that of the individual, this meshes with Job’s desire to be declared righteous before God. More probably, however, it refers to God’s righteousness, in the sense of the transformation that enables Job to act rightly for God.

God’s dealings with an individual may effect his deliverance from death and open up the possibility for further enjoyment of life. Elihu emphasizes that God’s dealings with an individual in this life are instructive, though he leaves room for punitive suffering as well. Elihu does not, however, really cover Job’s situation, for there is no punitive element in what has come upon Job. Elihu urges Job to consider what he is saying and to set out any difficulties he has with the argument because Elihu desires Job to be set right through God’s redemptive grace, but Elihu’s assumption that Job needs to be set right in this specific instance is mistaken. Ultimately, Job’s travails foreshadow the sufferings of Christ, who, though sinless, “learned obedience through what he suffered” and thus proved Himself to be rightly equipped to serve as high priest (Heb. 5:7–9). Through his suffering, Job will also be equipped to act in a priestly role and pray for his counselors (42:8).

After a pedantic introduction (vv. 2–4), Elihu quotes words from Job that are easy to refute (12:4; 13:18; 27:2, 6). His thesis is that no one is really innocent, so God denies no one justice (vv. 14, 15). The bulk of this second speech is a defense of God’s goodness and justice (vv. 10–30). Elihu closes with another condemnation of Job’s words and a call for repentance (vv. 31–37).

The expression implies that others are addressed as well as Job and his friends. This is quite possible since the reader does not learn Elihu was present and observing the earlier dialogues until ch. 32.

A fair representation of Job’s claim in 27:2. “I am in the right” (see 9:15, 20; 27:6) is a demand that he should be pronounced righteous, that is, innocent of any major sin commensurate with his suffering. The following two occurrences of “my right” take up the term of v. 4, “what is right,” an idea closer to “justice” or “just cause” (see 19:7; 27:2)., 6
Elihu accuses Job of having an insatiable propensity to expose himself to ridicule by maintaining his innocence while suffering as he is.

Elihu is probably not making allegations about Job’s previous conduct but is asserting that his present accusations against God render his speech and outlook indistinguishable from those of the wicked.

A number of passages are reflected here, but principally 21:15, though that is not Job’s own sentiment but his description of the outlook of the wicked. Job has, however, repeatedly argued that God treats the righteous and the wicked alike (see 9:22; 21:17; 24:1–12).

verse_quote: far be it from God that he should do wickedness.
note: For the next twenty-one verses Elihu expounds this theme. In moments of extreme stress Job said practically the opposite (10:3; 12:4–6; 21:7, 8; 24:1–12).

A clear statement of the retribution principle, which is not wrong in itself as long is it is not viewed simplistically. What is flawed is taking that principle as the exclusive key to understanding God’s present providential dealings.
Because God does not depend on anyone for His status, He is sovereign and necessarily in the right.

Elihu is right: God’s continual common grace is necessary for any of His creatures to continue to exist. However, the survival of any individual or of humanity as a whole is not a matter of just recompense for their deeds but is grounded in God’s inscrutable purposes., 15

Elihu turns to Job (“you” is singular in these verses) and takes up his query as to why the innocent do not see God’s judgment of the wicked (24:1). Elihu’s answer is that all, including those in positions of social prominence, are under God’s impartial scrutiny, though this is not always evident to the eyes of humanity.

Elihu points to God’s omniscience (v. 21 echoes Job’s expression in 31:4). He has no need to gather further facts to arrive at a verdict (vv. 21–24) and so does not need to respond to Job’s demand for a hearing. God overthrows the wicked suddenly (v. 25) and conspicuously (v. 26). Moreover, no one has the right to condemn God if He does not act immediately (v. 29). The ruler of the universe has to take into account far more than we can comprehend. God does act to prevent the godless from overturning His sovereign purpose (v. 30).
A difficult verse that seems to deal with Job’s complaint by asserting that God is acting as judge even though to human perception He is “quiet” and “hides his face.”

Elihu asks two questions, of which the first is posed in general terms. He asks if anyone suffering punishment for sin has ever repented. In v. 32 he supposes that the real nature of the offense may be unknown to the sufferer., 32

Elihu’s second question is pointedly directed to Job. He must decide whether to persist in his demands for divine explanation and restitution. “Declare what you know” (“keep to the facts”) rather than speculate about what has not been revealed. Elihu urges Job to abandon his wrongheaded thinking and to approach God in a respectful fashion.

In a further attempt to persuade Job, Elihu muses about the verdict of a hypothetical group of wise men who unsurprisingly echo Elihu’s viewpoint. The presuppositions of Job’s arguments are invalid (v. 35). If a thorough scrutiny of all that he has said were to occur, it would make clear that his thinking has become aligned with the spiritually rebellious (v. 36). Moreover, Job is acting disrespectfully to the wise by clapping his hands in derision to silence them and by making lengthy accusations against God (v. 37).

Elihu addresses Job and takes up his allegation that God has not rewarded him, even though Job is innocent of gross misconduct. Elihu defends divine sovereignty by arguing that God is not affected by Job’s sin or by his innocence (vv. 6, 7). Furthermore, God may withhold an answer to the pleas of mankind because of human pride (vv. 12, 13).

Elihu questions Job’s consistency in saying that God will vindicate him while at the same time saying it makes no difference whether he has lived a sinful life.

**35:2 to be just.** Lit. “in accordance with justice.”

**It is my right before God.** Lit. “my righteousness from God.” Presumably Job expects a divine verdict regarding his innocence.
This question resembles Eliphaz’s words in 22:3 but may be extrapolated from Job’s words in 9:14–31.
The heavens and the clouds are higher than Job; how much more so is God?

Elihu argues that what happens on earth is incapable of affecting the essential blessedness of God. Human claims of righteousness do not sway God, though He does respond to trust and faith. Elihu has not grasped that Job wants to see God’s ways vindicated in the prosperity of those who trust in Him., 7
Human sin does affect the sinner, and his personal conduct does make a difference to his life (see v. 3).

Job complained in ch. 23 that God has been indifferent to his situation and has not answered his prayers (24:12; 30:20). Elihu counters with some good advice (especially vv. 9–11). But some of it does not apply to Job (v. 12). In times of misery and hardship, people cry out for relief but not always with due recognition of who God is and what He can do. Their cries are self-centered, and do not acknowledge the blessings God has bestowed (v. 11). Cries for relief from distress are not the same as prayer.

verse_quote: who gives songs in the night.
note: God is able to give joy even in the darkest set of circumstances.
Without due recognition of who God is, cries to Him are spiritually empty. They express human arrogance and pride, and so God does not respond (see James 4:1–3)., 13

Elihu criticizes what Job has said and its effect on his relationship to God. Job is inconsistent in saying that he does not see God while also claiming to wait for Him and saying that his case is in God’s hands. His presumption leaves his pleas unanswered.

Elihu sets out Job’s earlier argument that God does nothing about wickedness (24:1–17). But Job meant only that God’s action need not be in this life. Elihu argues that Job’s speech was empty in that it was not based on a proper recognition of divine punishment of sin. Elihu views God as continuing to extend grace to Job.
Elihu argues that Job speaks presumptuously, without due recognition of God’s sovereign plan (see 34:35, 37) and that this is also God’s verdict (38:2).

In his final contribution, Elihu focuses on Job’s suffering from the perspective of God’s perfect righteousness and absolute power. He speaks of God’s justice and power in His dealings with mankind (36:1–26) and then of His sovereignty and benevolence in His dealings with nature (36:27–37:24). God’s instruction alerts people to their sin, and whoever ignores it does so at his own peril (37:24).
Elihu opens the speech with a wordy apology in which he reasserts his credentials (see 32:6–33:7; 36:1–4).

Elihu is full of self-confidence regarding his grasp of the situation. He is certain of his ability to proclaim God’s “righteousness,” probably here referring to God’s ability to deliver a correct verdict on human affairs.

verse_quote: one who is perfect in knowledge.
note: If Elihu is describing himself, this is sheer conceit. It may, however, be a divine epithet (see 37:16) with Elihu presenting himself as God’s spokesman.

Elihu struggles with Job’s complaint about the wicked who prosper and the righteous who suffer (v. 6). With this in mind, he dwells on God’s power, goodness, justice, and mercy. But all this is in the context of the simplistic view of suffering that views it as being always in direct proportion to sins while righteousness is always blessed. Only the last judgment will reveal this; cf. John 9:2, 3 with Rom. 2:6; 2 Cor. 5:10.

**36:5 Behold.** This focus particle occurs four times in this speech to introduce statements about God’s power (see vv. 22, 26, 30).

Elihu sides with the three friends in their understanding of divine retribution. God’s action toward the unrighteous and the righteous is to be seen in this life. As was clear in 27:13–23, Job affirms that God practices justice. However, he has argued that this might not happen in this life and that certainly God is not acting fairly in his case.
Elihu emphasizes the benefits God bestows on the righteous, making them the equal of kings.

God uses affliction to alert even the righteous to their sin and their arrogant self-sufficiency. If they respond in obedience, then they will once more enjoy prosperity (v. 11). Not listening to God will lead to death. Unlike the three friends, Elihu focuses on Job’s spiritual attitude and does not presume there is heinous sin from his past to be unmasked and confessed.
Possibly “cross the river” (33:18 note).

Elihu continues to argue that God’s justice is immediately evident in His dealings with “the godless” (see 8:13), who are spiritually insensitive and refuse to yield to God or cry out to Him. God also deals appropriately with the afflicted when He uses their suffering as a means of spiritual discipline and education (v. 15).
A reference to individuals who engage in depraved sexual rituals at idolatrous sanctuaries (see 1 Kin. 14:24; 15:12). A shameful end is described.

Elihu shifts his focus from general principles to Job’s particular situation and assures him of God’s good purpose in his suffering. He sternly admonishes Job to receive God’s divine discipline, with its promise of deliverance from distress. Job’s reaction to this experience of divine wrath will give proof of his true inner disposition.
The rendering of vv. 18–20 is difficult. Elihu asks Job to accept the great ransom of 33:24 and not persist in defying God and demanding that He act.

verse_quote: Do not long for the night.
note: Refers either to “night” as the time when people use the cover of darkness to sin (24:13–17) or to the night of death. Neither will provide adequate shelter for Job.
Job’s conduct in complaining against God is wrong. He should bear his affliction without complaint.

Elihu now returns to his opening thesis (v. 5) concerning the sovereignty of God, whose purpose is always good. God uses the circumstances of life to teach (v. 22), and no one is able to sit in judgment over Him (v. 23). It is pointless for Job to maintain his self-righteous stance over against Him. He should instead learn the lesson he is being taught and repent.
In view seems to be the heavenly display of God’s greatness. Job has shown his awareness of God’s greatness but not of his inconsistency in criticizing Him.
Elihu’s graphic description of God’s awesome majesty displayed in His control over the forces of nature is somewhat like God’s first speech (see ch. 38).
The scope of “judge” here is more general than giving a verdict. In view is the total administration of their affairs.
Probably a reference to the approaching storm.
A difficult passage to translate. Possibly the thought is that if the cattle are restive before the thunder of God, Job should much more take notice.

Elihu also is affected by the magnificence of the thunderstorm. It seems that there is an actual storm approaching, with which the whirlwind of ch. 38 is associated. The chapter division is probably introduced here because of Elihu’s reference to his own reaction.
The verb is plural, indicating that up to v. 14 Elihu is speaking also to Job’s companions.
The term implies that which is truly extraordinary and therefore beyond human comprehension. It has the same origin as “marvelous” (5:9; 9:10).
Sealing a document means that no more can be added to it. Extending that thought to the human hand implies that individuals are unable to work, possibly because of the bad weather being described.

Elihu may have in mind more than natural storms; he may be generalizing to include the storms of life.

**for love.** persistent, loyal love; here, seeking to reclaim through warning.

Here the link with the divine speeches (chs. 38–41) becomes more pronounced, as the young counselor begins to cross-examine Job about God’s power and righteousness. His concluding words anticipate the appearance of God in the heavens (vv. 21, 22).

verse_quote: we cannot draw up our case.
note: Elihu’s rhetorical questions have exposed Job’s ignorance of how God controls natural forces. It is therefore preposterous that mankind can draw up a watertight argument to overthrow God’s judgment. “Darkness” refers to lack of comprehension. The implication is that Job’s action in ch. 31 is deficient and necessarily misguided.

verse_quote: no one looks on the light.
note:
If looking at the sun in the heavens dazzles human vision, how much more so do human attempts to view the splendor of God.

**Out of the north.** Possibly a reference to the north as the home of the gods (see Ps. 48:2), an idea prevalent in the surrounding culture. The subject of the verb may be “God” or “gold.” If the former, the thought is that “He comes with golden splendor.”, 22

Elihu has warned Job to show humility before God and not to become narrow-minded in his self-perception and thus to fail to show due reverence and respect to God. In many respects, Elihu here sides with the theology of the friends’ simplistic principle of retribution.

In His appearance to Job, God does not mention the subject of Job’s suffering, much less give the reason for it. What the Lord says is far more important than Job’s suffering, which the Lord knows He will shortly remove. Nor does Job receive the bill of indictment he has wanted (31:35), for there is none. Job learns he must rest his case, including his desire for vindication, in the hands of a sovereign and good God, who is not his enemy (1 Pet. 4:19). God has come not to stand in the dock but to preside over the court. Job does not confront God; the Lord confronts him.

**38:1–40:2** The Lord calls on Job to withdraw his accusations against the Almighty by exposing his weakness and foolishness. The divine interrogation contains a measure of sympathy. God questions Job so that Job may come to a greater measure of self-knowledge. His lack of clarity about God reflects a lack of clarity regarding himself. In a series of questions about the natural world, the Lord reveals to Job just how little he actually knows. If Job does not understand God’s ways with nature, how can he understand His ways with mankind? Job has displayed impatience and presumption, of which he should repent. True piety is not based on comprehending all about God but on trust in His wisdom and goodness.

**38:1 the** LORD**.** The divine covenant name is used again, as in the prologue, showing that the author was an Israelite. Job and his counselors use other divine epithets such as “God” and “the Almighty.” Job 12:9 is the only place where Job or the counselors use the covenant name “Yahweh,” and some manuscripts have “God” even there. Job was evidently not an Israelite. The use of the name highlights the personal dealings of the Lord with Job as one in a saving relationship with Him.

**the whirlwind.** Presumably associated with the storm Elihu had seen coming (37:22).
God accuses Job of speaking without knowledge (see 34:35; 35:16) and therefore of obscuring what ought to be done in his situation.
Although God has appeared as Job requested, there is no doubt about who is in charge. Job had expected that he would be able to demand answers from God (31:35).

In His cross-examination of Job, the Lord reveals Himself as sovereign over the natural world. He is creator (38:4–15) of the earth (vv. 4–7), of the sea (vv. 8–11), and of day and night (vv. 12–15). He is Lord of inanimate nature (38:16–38) and of animate nature (38:39–39:30). What does Job know about these things? Job has to accept that he is the creature, not the Creator.

**38:4 Where were you.** Highlights Job’s finitude. He obviously was not around when God, as a master builder, constructed the earth. Since he did not see the plan, there are obvious gaps in his knowledge of its execution.
The irony here and in vv. 18, 21 is not sarcasm (intended to hurt), but a reminder that God is the creator.

For the personification of natural forces as God’s angels, see Ps. 104:4 and Heb. 1:7.

**morning stars.** Possibly Venus and Mercury. They are personified, not deified. “The sons of God” are angelic beings (1:6; 2:1). Both join in acclaiming the power and wisdom of the Creator (see Ps. 148:2, 3).
God controlled the sea and ordained its boundaries (Gen. 1:9, 10; Ps. 33:7; 104:9; Jer. 5:22). The origin of the oceans is described in terms of giving birth.
God determines the daily cycle of light and darkness and uses the change to curtail the activities of the wicked during the night.
The light of the wicked is darkness (Is. 5:20; Luke 11:35).
Job’s limitations are further exposed by listing locations he has never explored: the depths of the sea, the realm of the dead, and the wide expanse of territory throughout the earth.

The “gates” stand for dominion (Matt. 16:18). The Lord is sovereign over this invisible realm, which no living person has ever seen (17:16). According to the pagan religions of Canaan, the god Mot was ruler of the realm of the dead, but Job knows otherwise (see 26:6).
Light and darkness are personified as living in houses, but Job does not know where and he cannot tell where the sun goes when it sets (vv. 19–20).
This is irony, affirming that Job was not present when these aspects of creation were instituted. Only God is eternal (see 36:26).
Job does not know how snow or hail originate. They are viewed as kept in divine storehouses and released by God as a means of intervention in earthly affairs (v. 23; see Josh. 10:11).
. Probably refers to lightning, since this section is about weather. “The east wind” is the storm wind coming from the desert.

Again God puts Job in his place by stressing who is in control of rain and ice.

**38:25 cleft a channel.** Not a course for a river to flow but a path in the sky along which the rain clouds come.

In a world where rainwater is precious, God impresses on Job His sovereign freedom to do what perplexes those who don’t appreciate the distinctions between the sovereign God and themselves. Nature does not exist simply for mankind.

verse_quote: bind ... Pleiades ... loose the cords of Orion.
note: God alone has dominion over the cosmic forces that constrain the cluster of stars called “Pleiades” in the constellation of Taurus and those making up the belt of the hunter Orion. Job acknowledged this in 9:9.

An unknown constellation, not mentioned in 9:9.

**the Bear.** It is uncertain which star with “its children” makes up this constellation to which Job refers.
Job’s inability to direct rain (v. 34) and lightning (v. 35) further demonstrates the limitations of his power and knowledge.

The Hebrew word translated “mind” occurs only here, and its meaning has been in question since ancient times. In one traditional translation, the verse asks who gave wisdom to “the ibis” and “the rooster,” birds that were thought to announce the coming of the rain and the flooding of the Nile.

The questions shift from inanimate to animate creation, a sampling of God’s creatures great and small. Beginning here with lions and ravens, the full list comprises five animals and four birds (38:39–39:30). Job does not sustain the animal realm; God does (see Luke 12:24), and therefore He will surely not neglect the needs of human beings.

verse_quote: Do you know ... Do you observe . . . Can you number.
note: God reminds Job of His creative, wise, and sustaining work even in the barren hills where man can scarcely live. This reminds Job of his ignorance by contrast. The “mountain goat” is probably the ibex, which retreats into inaccessible areas to give birth., 2

This creature was greatly admired for its freedom and its ability to live in “the arid plain” and “the salt land” around the Dead Sea (v. 6). Job has no ability to control the movements of such animals or to sustain them.

This now-extinct animal, the aurochs, was already rare in Palestine in Job’s day. These large, powerful creatures resisted domestication. They were hunted to extinction in the ancient Near East by the Egyptians and the Assyrians, though they survived longer in Europe, where they also became extinct. The aurochs is the ancestor of modern domesticated cattle.

The flightless ostrich may have wings, but their wings are not used as expected. “Of love” may well be a reference to “a stork” or “heron,” which nests in trees (Ps. 104:17) and has strong wings (Zech. 5:9). In contrast, the ostrich nests on the ground, exposing her young to danger. The mother bird may desert her nestlings (Lam. 4:3).

verse_quote: she laughs at the horse and his rider.
note: Though the ostrich cannot fly, it runs faster than a horse. Job has complained of paradoxes in his life; God shows him natural paradoxes that are resolved only in the secret (or revealed) purposes of the self-existent God.

verse_quote: Do you give the horse his might.
note: Probably this is the war horse, by reputation the strongest and most intelligent animal but still only partly domesticated. Since Job’s strength is inferior to that of the horse, he is unable to compete with the creator of the horse.

The final lesson from the natural realm concerns birds of prey. “Toward the south” (v. 26) refers to the migratory instinct of the sparrow hawk, which passed through the region on its way south. In light of v. 30, the vulture may be intended here.

verse_quote: his eyes behold it from far away.
note: In addition to the mysterious migratory instinct of birds (v. 26), these words speak of the phenomenal eyesight of eagles. If Job cannot understand or regulate so many features of the created realm, he is in no position to call God to answer for His conduct. Furthermore, the natural realm witnesses to God’s concern and provision for it. This runs contrary to Job’s allegation that God is uncaring and distant.

This conclusion of the first speech should be compared to its opening with a rebuking question (38:2) and a challenge that Job respond (38:3). Both are directed toward Job’s bold but erroneous utterances during his moments of doubt.

**40:2** Job had viewed God as contending with him (10:2; 23:6), but now God turns the tables on Job and demands that he answer what is put to him (38:3).
Job abandons his obsession with being vindicated. It is his turn to speak, but he has no argument to present. He is brought low before the Almighty.

Job has become aware of his insignificance before the Creator, who controls all. There is no response Job can give. He abandons his earlier self-confidence (10:2; 13:22; 14:15). However, silence before God is not necessarily linked to repentance. Job still seems petulant, overwhelmed by what God has said but not prepared to give up his defiant remonstrance. Even so, God does not give up on Job but speaks to him again.

The same introduction (cf. 40:6 with 38:1) points to the awesome location of the speech. The Lord opens His second discourse (40:6, 7) as He did in 38:1–3, but here he challenges Job with a new line of reasoning about whether God is just in judging the wicked. In His first speech, God revealed Himself as Lord of nature, but here He shows Himself to be Lord of the moral realm. Job cannot act to administer justice. He should be content to leave such matters in God’s hands. The divine speech is vehement, stripping away Job’s pride.
This section emphasizes God’s power over pride and wickedness (vv. 11, 12).

Heb. “nullify my justice.” Not only is Job asserting his innocence; he is challenging the integrity of God’s administration of the world.

**Will you condemn me.** Job has been prepared to judge God and pronounce a guilty verdict (19:6) because of his sense of self-righteousness and the incomprehensibility of certain aspects of his situation as he perceived it.

Ironic commands meant to underline Job’s incapacity to acquire for himself even the garb of divine majesty, far less exercise real power; they highlight his incapacity to judge God’s dealings with mankind.

Job had complained that God does not punish the wicked (21:29–31; 24:1–17)—at least not quickly enough—so God ironically suggests that Job undertake the task and so exposes Job’s arrogant presumption. If Job could perform that role, God would grant that Job possessed the capacity to remedy his situation. Otherwise Job should rest content with God’s way of acting.
Job needs more than vindication before others. He has wronged God. It is his relationship with God that is at stake.

The monsters in these verses, Behemoth and Leviathan, probably represent forces of evil that God can control but before which Job is helpless. As to whether these are real or mythical animals, it seems best to regard them as hyperbolized portraits of something real in the natural realm. However, they also function in an ancient Near Eastern context as symbols of chaos, death, and evil. The power of these animals has sinister and dangerous overtones. If Job cannot control these animals, how can he grapple with the mysterious powers of evil that they represent?

**40:15 Behemoth.** Since Job is called on to look at Behemoth, which God created, it may be that a real creature is in view. The Behemoth has many points of similarity with a hippopotamus. It is herbivorous (v. 15) and therefore not a threat to other animals (v. 20). The hippopotamus’s stomach muscles are far stronger than those of an elephant (v. 16). Its tail, though relatively small, stiffens when the animal is startled or running (v. 17). It was the largest mammal known in the region (v. 19). The Hebrew root is used for “cattle,” but the plural form here implies “the beast beyond comparison,” particularly in terms of its size and strength. Parts of the description, especially v. 19, go beyond any natural creature such as the hippopotamus or the crocodile. In any event, the Lord’s speech indicates that whatever the forces of this creature, it is no more than a plaything in comparison to His unfathomable power.
The habitat described may be the marshy ground near Lake Huleh, which lay to the north of the Sea of Galilee.

The description fits a hippopotamus lying almost totally submerged in water. Its eyes and nostrils do not present a target that a hunter could use to spear and kill it. Less probable is the idea of a domesticated Behemoth led around with a hook in its nose.

Another creature similar to Behemoth, but whereas Behemoth is a beast from the land, Leviathan comes from the sea (see Rev. 13). Leviathan is given the longest treatment of any creature and is even more terrifying than Behemoth. It is mentioned as a climax; it attacks humans (v. 8). The description of its back (vv. 13, 15–17, 23), its teeth (v. 14), its chest and undersides (vv. 24, 30), and the way it causes turmoil in the water (v. 31) all fit with a crocodile as the origin of the representation. Again, the poetic description is anchored in nature but symbolizes something even more terrifying. Like Leviathan in Is. 27:1 and Ps. 74:14, the imagery denotes threatening powers in the heavenly and earthly realms (Rev. 12:7; 13:1).

**41:1–11** The implements available to mankind are insufficient for capturing Leviathan. It is so fierce it cannot be tamed as a pet, and no one is able to talk with one (vv. 3–5).

God created and controls these massive creatures, so His might is far greater than theirs. Arguing from the lesser to the greater, if Job or any other human cannot dominate the creatures of God, how do they think they can supervise and direct Him?

It is unlikely that Leviathan is a mythical dragon that breathes fire. It is more probably a hyperbolic portrayal of a crocodile emerging from water. “His sneezings flash forth light” may imply no more than the water vapor it expels when it clears its nostrils after being submerged, seen against the sun as spray.
If the crocodile’s presence and movement terrifies strong men, how does Job think he is able to contend with the creator of such an awesome beast?
The point of the comparison is uncertain; perhaps it is to the foam and froth on the surface of a container of boiling liquid.

This fits exactly the lines introducing Behemoth and Leviathan in 40:11, 12. Job cannot humble the arrogant wicked by looking down on them (40:11–14), but Leviathan can. How much more can God look down on Job’s proud assertiveness against the Lord Himself? If Job cannot tame these creatures whose might makes them seem contemptuous of other beings and whose presence conveys a constant threat of destructive force, his posturing against God is quite absurd. God, the creator, can deal with these animals and any evil they may symbolically represent. In fact, that is exactly the case throughout the book: Job has (unknowingly) been engaged in a struggle with Satan, whom he has no power to defeat. However, Satan and his forces of evil have no more power than God allows them. He is able to treat them like tame household pets.

Appropriately, Job is now more than humbled: he must repent for his rash words and doubting of God’s justice during his deepest suffering and his audacity in thinking he could institute proceedings against God. Because of his experience, his repentance is unforced and sincere as he acknowledges the full dimensions of God’s sovereignty and confesses his folly in questioning God’s goodness and justice.
See theological note “Omnipresence and Omnipotence” at Jer. 23:24.

Job quotes God’s question in 38:2 to admit his fault in speaking beyond what he knows. He responds to both discourses, not just the second one. He now accepts his limitations and concedes God’s sovereign wisdom.
Job again quotes God, this time the challenge with which God began His two speeches (38:3; 40:7). In doing so, Job is admitting that he cannot answer God’s questions.

verse_quote: but now my eye sees you.
note: Job cannot see physically through the whirlwind out of which God speaks (38:1; 40:6); he expresses a deeper meaning. He had known God with words, but he now experiences His living presence in his inner being. He meets Him as Savior and friend and, above all, God. His disposition to argue through ignorance and presumption has been overwhelmed and removed.

More probably, “I reject myself,” “I recall my former opinions.” Acknowledging how faulty and rash his speech has been, Job rejects the accusations he had made against God. Throwing dust and ashes over oneself was an accepted expression of humility (2:12 and note). Job grieves over the offense of his sin and is truly repentant. While not accepting his friends’ argument that his great suffering has been caused by great sin, Job admits he has not maintained his initially correct attitude toward God (1:21, 22; 2:10) but has become unwarrantably resentful and accusatory (see 34:37). Now Job is willing to trust God, accepting that His ways, while inscrutable, are nevertheless right—even in the calamities that had engulfed him.

The drama introduced in the prologue now comes full circle. The epilogue is written in prose, matching the introductory chapters.

**42:7–9** The Lord rebukes Job’s counselors and accepts Job’s prayers on their behalf. As the eldest among them, Eliphaz represents the others.

**42:7 My anger.** The Lord’s attitude toward the friends is similar to Elihu’s reaction in 32:3.

**what is right.** Since God has rebuked (and forgiven) Job for his sinful words, why does He say that Job said what was right while the counselors did not? On the one hand, Job throughout was determined to speak honestly before God. He did not succumb to the threat of disowning Him. On the other hand, though the counselors sincerely tried to defend God and their words were often formally blameless, they were less than upright and honest. The counselors failed in their arrogant assumption of why Job was suffering and in falsely accusing Job of sins of which he was not guilty. They thought they knew all about God, when actually their views were inadequate. That God accepts Job’s prayer on their behalf indicates His gracious forgiveness of them also.

**my servant Job.** This phrase, repeated four times in vv. 7, 8, emphasizes Job’s restored position as devoted and obedient to God, enjoying fellowship with Him (see 1:8).

We often assume that praying for one’s detractors is teaching from the NT, but it is here in Job. In this way Job foreshadows Christ, who, when nailed to the cross, prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).

The sequence in these verses is significant. The friends are first brought back to God through the instrumentality of Job’s intercessory prayer on their behalf. It is in his restored capacity as the servant of the Lord that Job acts. He is then further blessed in that he is abundantly honored by the Lord.

“Bless” reintroduces a term used six times in the prologue, as Job is restored and those who refused to be near him in his dark hour (19:13–20) are forgiven. The number of animals he possesses is double what he lost (v. 10; 1:3), and his seven sons and three daughters replace his family who died. Commentators have objected to this restoration, since so many through the ages have suffered without experiencing such blessing. But God allowed Satan to strike Job to prove that His servant would remain true. The reader knows that Satan was proved a liar: Job never cursed God (1:11; 2:5), and God was glorified. It was the good pleasure of God to reward His servant. The “steadfastness of Job” was known to God (James 5:11). Job’s cry, “I will argue my ways to his face” (13:15) can be compared with Jacob’s, “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Gen. 32:26).
